en: Oṃ, salutations to the Gurus beginning with Śiva!
He who, possessing power, assumes three forms in the three states and,
by means of his power, effects the emergence, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe.
I offer salutations to that Śiva, the Supreme Self, who consists of pure nectar,
and who is the supreme Brahman, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
To Maheśvara, the God of gods, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa,
Hara who was sporting together with Pārvatī and his attendants.
Seeing that the god was delighted by his desire for the welfare of living beings,
Pārvatī quickly descended from his lap and grasped his feet.
Having gratified the Supreme Lord with supreme devotion, she questioned him.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the world, Master of the universe!
That great marvel which has been performed by you is truly astonishing.
O God, O Supreme Lord of the entire world, yet that secret which is difficult to understand and difficult to propitiate has not been revealed to me.
In the month of Kārttika, there is nothing for me among the gods, nor among the Gaṇas;
indeed, there is nothing among the Yogīśvarīs, the Mothers, the Ṛṣis, or the Yogins.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, O Master, if you are well-pleased with me today,
I, having sought refuge, pray that you deign to tell it to me in its entirety.
Having heard these words of the goddess, the Blessed One, with a serene countenance, spoke.
The Blessed One said:
"What, what do you say, O fair-hipped one, that dwells in your heart at the end of our secret?"
"I shall tell you everything without doubt, O sinless one, for I have been gratified by you.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, such a wonderful and delightful marvel, which brings about many wonders, has never been heard by me; I am now hearing it.
O All-pervading One, with a serene countenance, you who bring about supreme bliss;
O Blessed One, out of your lack of selfishness, you should explain this to me.
Since that divine eye consisting of water is seen everywhere,
how did the fierce fire, the burner at the end of time, arise from it?
O Lord, what was that terrible act committed by Vahni, who, out of a desire to see Kāla, reduced Pitṛṣā to ashes merely by being seen?
The entire world, from Brahmā down to the goddess Chāmunda, was set ablaze;
likewise, O Supreme Lord, Kāma was consumed by Your mere play.
O Lord, that which was seen by no one else in the fire of the wrathful eye was performed by the God of Gods, causing great amazement.
Indeed, within the eye of the gods resides fire; other than you, by whom could it be seen?
Or rather, how is it that the eye itself is not perceived as being composed of fire?
O Lord of the World, by that very eye which is entirely composed of nectar, you indeed cause the entire expanding universe to be nourished in an instant.
O Lord, you gladden me with your very gracious eye,
which is as radiant as the form of nectar and brings nourishment to the entire world.
Therefore, from what does fire arise that resembles the fire of cosmic destruction?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this to me in brief.
The Blessed One said:
"O beloved, you ask this out of excessive curiosity; listen to what there is within my eyes—namely, the fire and the unsurpassed nectar."
I shall explain all of that through the method of yoga; listen, O beloved, to that which is one's own essential nature—pure, all-pervading, and facing every direction.
Abiding within all beings as the life-force in all living creatures,
it is attainable through yoga, difficult to propitiate, and hard to reach for those of unrefined self.
My own supreme state is self-cognizable and possesses its own inherent power;
that power is the power of all powers, and it is indeed the strength of the strong.
Then, I spoke of all that is eternal and immovable, consisting of splendor and vital energy;
for the supreme power is indeed Sāma, inseparable and born of its own nature.
She is to be known as the heat within fire and as the form of the sun, like the sun itself;
she is the causal power of the entire world.
Therein reside the qualities such as omniscience, both manifest and unmanifest;
she herself is the nature of will and knowledge, yet she is forgotten by those who possess qualities such as knowledge.
The six qualities, beginning with knowledge, which reside there and manifest forth—
she indeed is the Great Form (Mahārūpā), established as the one and only action, considered to be Action itself.
She effects and transforms the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*;
thus, my power—consisting of will, knowledge, and action—is called *icchā-jñāna-kriyā*.
The sun and moon, as well as fire, constitute the conception of the three abodes;
it is for that purpose that the conception of my three eyes is seen here.
Having illuminated it by means of burning and nourishing, I bring about creation, maintenance, and dissolution; I fashion that very body.
All is filled with its power, augmented by my own splendor;
it is the supreme nectar of the eyes, whose form consists of will, knowledge, and action.
That supreme power is the highest abode, which consists of the supreme nectar;
it is this very supreme bliss within the body, that supreme state.
This is that partless knowledge, pure and the most excellent eye.
By him it was proclaimed as "Victorious over Death," the bestower of liberation for all;
O Goddess, that supreme [mantra] grants success and bestows release from all suffering.
The God who removes all diseases, Śiva who consists of all that is auspicious,
the eternal subduer of poverty, the conqueror of death, whose face is turned in every direction.
Unfailing, stainless, peaceful, all-pervading, and abiding in all things;
[it is] like ten thousand times ten million suns and ten thousand times ten thousand fires.
Since by its splendor it makes all other [splendors] worth not even a sixteenth part,
it is therefore composed entirely of light and is invincible to both gods and demons.
By that fire from my eye, I shall surely burn everything away in an instant;
by that very same [fire], I again perform nourishment and manifestation.
Therefore, nothing else more supreme than that is seen even by the wise;
that very [power] is the fierce weapon consisting of missiles, the supreme means of deliverance for the individual soul.
This weapon, which brings about the destruction of enemies, has been described;
for all living beings, it is their weapon at the end of their life.
That single heroic power, spread out infinitely through various divisions,
is my own Mahāpāśupata and that Sudarśana of Viṣṇu.
The Brahma-staff belongs to Brahmā, and each of all [the others] has their own respective weapon;
that weapon appears in many forms and is manifold in its various types.
My virility was bestowed upon the gods in the form of Sura;
by that [Sura], through the power of knowledge belonging to Yogeśī, this entire world is pervaded.
For those who are afraid, she is the supreme protection; for those who bathe here, there is the highest fearlessness;
and for those afflicted by enemies, she is certainly the supreme bestower of liberation.
Or what is the use of speaking at length with such repetition, O Sundarī?
Whatever is exceedingly fierce or even devoid of splendor—
Indeed, that very [reality] which is grace, the giver of boons, and the manifestation of the highest good, is that which is to be known;
it is immeasurable, knowledge, the mantra, and possessed of great power.
O Goddess, I have today told you that which is the protector of all beings and must always be kept secret by me; yet you ask about it once again.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Tantra," in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, concerning the ritual procedure for conquering death and attaining immortality. || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
If it is thus that I have heard from the mouth of the God of Gods about this supreme, peaceful, immeasurable vigor, which is the abode of virtues and bestows grace upon all;
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who bestow grace upon the worlds:
all this—gods, humans, and animals—is born from the three wombs.
Distressed by mental and physical ailments and fears, afflicted by the dangers of poison and malevolent spirits,
beset by hundreds of untimely deaths, and possessed by fever, cough, and consumption.
O Lord, since beings such as Brahmins and others in the world of humans are born of the elements and are beset by hundreds of miseries and defects, how can there be happiness for them?
In accordance with the nature of the age,
those endowed with strength, augmented by your own fiery power, seek to destroy their own lifespan according to its measure.
Tormented by hundreds of various diseases and other afflictions,
[this was taught] out of compassion for their benefit and for the welfare of all living beings.
The means by which the Lord of the World is addressed in every way—
by whatever method, whether through the yoga of knowledge or through mantra— [is explained].
"O Lord of Gods, tell me that means which you perceive.
Having heard these words of the Goddess, Śiva, the benefactor of the world, laughed repeatedly.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, possessed by excessive compassion, you ask me this;
I have never been asked by anyone, nor has anything ever been told by me to anyone.
That which is proclaimed as the eye within all eyes has been perceived by me through a certain portion of my own being, though it is extremely difficult for others to perceive;
today I shall explain to you that supreme and eternal reality in its threefold form.
Accessible through the knowledge of mantra and yoga, bestowing liberation and the supreme accomplishment,
I shall first describe that which consists of mantra, endowed with the threefold accomplishment.
Endowed with its limbs and its own mudrā, it is the supreme provider of protection everywhere against the hosts of bhūtas,
yakṣas, grahas, unmādas, śākinīs, and yoginīs.
[He was surrounded] by Bhaginīs, Rudramātṛs, Ḍāvyas, Ḍāmarakas, and others;
by Rūpikās, Apasmāras, and also numerous Piśācas.
Even if they have been seized by tens of millions of Brahma-rākṣasas, grahas, and other spirits, or if they are assailed by untimely deaths and threatened by the noose of Time;
Kings, princes, and royal consorts by the many,
as well as all living beings beginning with Brahmins, were afflicted by the fear of every kind of defect.
I shall now describe that by the mere remembrance of which one is liberated:
in a further location that is level, delightful, and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum.
In a place rich with the fragrance of camphor and scented with saffron water,
the preceptor, his soul exceedingly joyful and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum, [should perform the rite].

Adorned with ornaments such as the *uṣṇīṣa* and others, the one of great intelligence should fashion an eight-petaled lotus and draw the *mātṛkā* there. The three bodies (*tritanu*) should be written in the center, and one should write the eight groups of consonants (*varga*) starting from the east.
One should worship with supreme devotion using an abundance of flowers, incense, and water offerings;
then, O Goddess, the Mother of Mantras should extract the most excellent mantra.
The syllable *viśva* is the beginning, the syllable *viśvarūpa* is the end, and the syllable *amṛta* is the petal;
with the sound *sva*, the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) should unite Śiva in one place.
By this [mantra], everything is strung together like clusters of jewels on a thread;
from this [mantra] have arisen the seventy-seven million presiding deities.
The fire (Citrabhānu) is situated at the end of the foot, with the interior of the crescent moon;
it is placed above the goad, extending transversely and joined upwards.
This is that supreme light; this is that supreme nectar.
This is declared to be the supreme nectar, renowned throughout the world.
Endowed with a digit of nectar, resembling the full moon—
this is the supreme abode, this is the supreme state.
This is the supreme vigor, this is the supreme nectar;
it is the highest splendor among splendors, the most excellent light among lights.
O God, the Lord is the eternal cause of the entire world;
he is its creator, its maker, and its destroyer, and there is no one more powerful than him in this world.
For this is indeed the abode of mantras and the locus of all qualities of accomplishment;
now I shall describe the ancillaries by which one who is prepared attains success.
The syllable situated in the middle of *kṛtānta* (the letter *ma*), followed by the king of the gods (*su*) and the one that follows it (*ra*),
with the head ending in *prabhañjana* (*ya*), is established in the heart of all.

That which is joined with the fire-mantra (RA) at its beginning and conjoined with the Praṇava (OM) is the Head; that which is joined with the end of the wind-mantra (YA) and Māyā (HRĪM) is known as the Topknot.
It is profoundly tranquil, situated above the Lord, and joined with the six [faces];
likewise, it is endowed with Śiva, Śakti, and Nāda, and is the supreme path.
The Praṇava preceded by Sabhairava, the Sadāgati residing in the head,
and the Netramantra, which is most formidable and the destroyer of all sins.
This weapon is proclaimed as being joined with the *ajīvakaṭa*;
it is declared to be the six limbs that have issued forth from the King of Mantras.
Thus ends the second chapter, the procedure for extracting the mantra, within the Mṛtyuñjaya section of the Amṛtīśa-vidhāna, which is the essence of the compendium of all streams.
The Lord said:
Now I shall describe the sacrifice by which the king of mantras is perfected.
First, one should perform a bath that destroys all sins.
O Goddess of gods, having extracted the earth with the Astra-mantra, the knower of mantras,
having performed purification as prescribed, should thereafter perform his bath.
The feet, the shanks, and the hips are purified by three, three, and three [repetitions] respectively; through the internal application of these seven, the mind is purified.
Having consecrated the earth seven times with the Astra-mantra, the knower of mantras should heat it in the sun's rays and subsequently smear his body with it.
For the purpose of pacifying obstacles, one should recite [the mantra] while washing [the hands] within the water;
then, one should form three portions of clay with the left hand.
One should cast [water] consecrated with the Astra-mantra in all directions and designate the root [mantra] as the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Having smeared the body with the Anga-mantras, one should recite the mantra while submerged within the water and then rinse.
Having crossed over the root [mantra] with one's power, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) in due order;
then, having tied the topknot and recollected the topknot, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the mantras.

Having gathered at the sacred ford (tīrtha) and gratified the gods, the ancestors, the seers, humans, and the assembly of elemental beings according to the procedure prescribed for sacrifice, one should enter [the ritual].
One should worship Āśāmātrī and Gaṇa, as well as Lakṣmī, Nandin, and Gaṅgā;
then one should worship Mahākāla, Yamunā, and Dehalī.
Having performed the expulsion of obstacles (vighna-proccāṭana) and the binding of the directions (digbandha) with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and the weapon-mantra (astra),
one should establish the Power (Śakti) preceded by the Support (Ādhāra) for the sake of one’s own seat.
Having sat down, one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) in due order;
there, one should commence concentration (dhāraṇā) simultaneously with the processes of drying and so forth.
One should visualize the binding of the directions there as impure and belonging to the six treasuries;
one should remember that only pure consciousness, which has entered into emptiness, is present there.
Neither "I" exists nor does "another" exist; here, that which is to be meditated upon is revealed:
the mind, having become of one flavor, is deeply absorbed in the state of bliss.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the seat situated upon the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti)—
a lotus like the nectar of the earth, illuminated by the orb of the moon.

Afterwards, one should sprinkle the previously fashioned form with the nectar arising from the collection of digits (kalās); however, one should not perform this at the root in the state of the Tattvas.
Then, one should again place the limbs upon the body with both hands;
and through the yoga of meditation, one should contemplate the mantra as well as the sense of self-identity.
Then, having formed the Dhenu-mudrā or likewise the Padma-mudrā,
one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods within oneself, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Resembling a pure pearl, with a luster equal to a crystal on a bright day,
resembling the kunda flower, the moon, or cow’s milk— such is the Lord who is like me;
adorned with white ornaments, possessing the beauty of the bright autumn moon and other such whiteness.
His limbs were smeared with white sandalwood paste and greyed by the powder of camphor;
he was immersed in the vast, surging waves of the shimmering nectar of the moon.
Seated in the middle of a moon mandala, with one face and three eyes,
he is seated upon a white lotus, established in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana).
Four-armed and large-eyed, with hands holding a jujube fruit and the gesture of fearlessness,
resembling the full moon, pure white, and filled as if with nectar.
One should visualize [the deity] holding a water-pot (kalaśa) in the left hand, which causes the nourishment of the world and is as full as the moon.
One should meditate upon him as worshipped with entirely white offerings;
what need is there for much speaking here? He is the ocean of nectar itself.
From that very [source] has arisen the nectar that sustains the entire universe;
one should then contemplate it as resembling a wish-fulfilling gem through its various manifestations.
Gentle, fierce, and likewise terrible, deformed according to the distinction of their moods;
Sadāśiva, Bhairava, Ranta, Cuṇḍu, and Vīranāyaka.
For in whatever form the practitioner then remembers Him,
the Lord becomes identical with that very form, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the deity with auspicious mental flowers within the heart-lotus for the sake of all accomplishments; thereafter, one should perform worship externally.
Worship with mental flowers is considered auspicious by the practitioner;
it is free from ritual remains, supremely pure, bestows liberation, grants spiritual accomplishments, and is auspicious.
Therefore, with every effort, one should first certainly perform the mental sacrifice;
only afterwards should it be performed with elaborate material offerings.
In one's own home, in a temple, at a confluence, on a mountain peak,
or on a highly auspicious spot of ground, such as a beautiful cluster of lotuses.
One should draw a variegated mandala, adorned with white lines,
having four doors and four corners, perfectly level and delightful to the mind.
In the midst of that [palace], which was endowed with both beauty and splendor, was a lunar disc,
resembling the full moon and graced by a garland of radiant rays.
In its center is a desired eight-petalled lotus, brilliantly white like the moon,
endowed with variegated filaments and an excellent golden pericarp.
And in the very center of that, one should cause the Lord of Gods to descend from his own abode;
then one should invoke the God who is conceived as having three bodies.
One should assign the limbs (aṅgas) to the petals according to the divisions starting from the southeast (āgneya),
and worship them with white offerings, flowers, garments, and ointments.

One should worship with various and wonderful food offerings, with excellent and well-perfumed incenses, and with pleasing drinks and diverse snacks, according to the distinctions of one's inner disposition.
O Dear One, one should worship for the sake of pacification with entirely white offerings;
for the sake of nourishment, one should sacrifice with many mixed materials prepared as the necessary provisions.
Thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the specific requirements of the rite,
on a beautifully adorned altar that is circular, square, or has three ridges.
Then, in a pit measuring one cubit (hastamātra), with six limbs and three upper ridges,
the middling [pit] is formed by four [units] starting from the middle, while the lowest is formed by twelve limbs.
Then, one should dig a pit one cubit deep;
the rim should be one finger-breadth wide, and the navel, resembling an *aśvattha* leaf, should be nine fingers in size.
In length it should be one finger-breadth, and in width it should be proportionate to its middle and tip;
this is prescribed for a *sāhasrika* (thousand-fold) oblation, while for an *ayuta* (ten-thousand-fold) oblation, it is considered to be double that size.
By performing three times five hundred oblations, that rite is prescribed as being tripled;
a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics is indeed recommended for the Lakṣahoma.
For obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, as well as for pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), a circular [mandala] is prescribed;

it brings peace in all directions. For one desiring prosperity (śrī), a square [mandala] is recommended according to the previously mentioned measurement, having observed the distinctions between the ritual acts.
The consecrations (saṃskāras) of this fire-pit (kuṇḍa) should be performed with the Astra-mantra:
subduing (adhaḥkaraṇa), lifting up (uddhāra), scattering (abhikṣepa), and filling (prapūraṇa).
Sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and likewise smearing—
the preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be performed with the syllable Om (praṇava).
One should fashion the abode of Vāgīśī at a crossroads or within a gambling enclosure;
furthermore, the vehicle of Vāgīśī is [represented] by a sword or by the syllable Om (praṇava).
One must perform the sprinkling with water three times,
the striking with the Astra-mantra, and the consecration according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
By means of Kauṇḍilī, who is the very nature of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), one should conceive of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
one should then conceive of Fire there as being the very nature of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
Taking the fire placed in a vessel and consecrated by the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras),
one should perform the inspection and other rites with the Astra-mantra and the veiling with the Kavaca-mantra.
Having offered five oblations with the *praṇava* for the purification of the materials and so forth,
one should thereafter perform the invocation of the universal fire (*viśvāgnipādana*) and cause it to circulate three times.
Then, having agitated the seed-form, the Fire, the Supreme Lord within oneself,
as well as Māyā and Yogeśī, one should dissolve them into the womb; then,
once the entire universe has been made circular within the fire, one should perform worship with the *praṇava*.
First, that [consecration] should be performed upon her face, and thereafter the sacraments for Nala:
namely, the impregnation rite (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
In the Viśvāgni fire of the conceptualization of the mouth, one performs the conceptualization of the boundaries, the neck, and so forth;
likewise, here [are performed] the birth-rite (jātakarman), the rite of first going out (niṣkramaṇa), and the naming ceremony (nāmakalpanā).
The six limbs, beginning with the heart, should be performed in their proper sequence;
furthermore, those consecrations beginning with the topknot (cūḍā) are performed by means of a single final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
The knower of the ritual procedure should perform all the consecratory rites (saṃskāras) in the fire with the root mantra; therein, he should conceive [the fire] as consisting of Śiva and Śakti.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made sturdy from trees that produce milky sap;
however, for rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), those originating from auspicious trees are recommended.
Otherwise, according to the distinction of substances and in accordance with the intended purpose,
the measurement of the *sruc* or *sruva* ladle is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in size.
The staff rises from the pot with a circumference of six parts;
its pedestal-top is four finger-breadths wide, and that pedestal is like the interior of a lotus.
In the middle of the staff, a circular section two fingers long and half a finger in height should be fashioned,
filled with various artistic designs; the pedestal (vedikā) should be made eight fingers high, beautiful and symmetrical on all four sides.

At the bottom, a lotus is placed with its ends facing upward; it should be joined with five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula). That excavation should be made one finger-breadth deep, and above that, a circular rotation [should be made], adorned with *tilaka* marks measuring half a finger-breadth.
Its four sides are provided with four corners;
it is considered to be constructed through various designs and the expertise of artisans.
The neck should be made one aṅgula, divided into three parts;
then, on both sides, a beautiful face measuring seven aṅgulas should be fashioned.
On the two sides of the length, however, one should gradually reduce by two parts;
at the tip of the face, there should likewise be two parts out of three on the two sides.
One should rotate and cause it to be known [as] the measure of the little finger;
one should make it gradually deeper and deeper until the interval between the tips of the faces [is reached].
Likewise, an auspicious and variegated arrangement should be made on both sides;
it should likewise be fashioned from the portion of one's own self on both sides.

The *sruva* ladle should be one cubit (*hasta*) in length; its base should have three prongs, its middle and tip bases should be marked with lotuses, and its neck should be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in circumference.
It should be four finger-breadths long, with two well-rounded openings at the tip;
one should fashion it so that it has a hollow like the joint of a thumb, shaped like a cow’s hoofprint.
The base should be circular, measuring one *kaniṣṭhā* finger-breadth in depth;
it should be fashioned according to the words of the Sun and have its opening filled with gold.
The full *sruva* ladle consists of four *pala*s; the *śakti* is the *sruva* ladle, O Śiva, while the *kriyāśakti* is the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the *jñānaśakti* is the fire-pole (*nala*).
Having thus performed [the preliminary rites] according to the rules, one should afterwards perform the fire-oblation (homa).
The oblation should be offered with sesame seeds mixed with milk, sugar, and clarified butter.
Great peace shall arise at that very moment; there is no doubt in this.
First, one should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya), and then the subsequent fire-oblation (homa).
Placing [the vessel] on the fire, taking it off, stirring it, setting it down,
then inspecting it, and thereafter performing the lustration (nirājana) with the weapon-mantra.
The encircling with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), as well as the rising and falling (utplava-saṃplava),
the worship with the Astra-mantra at the root, and likewise the immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).
One should prepare the darbha-grass mat, the seats, and the enclosing sticks with the appropriate mantras,
and one should invoke the Sun, the Moon, and Fire with the Praṇava.
One should visualize one's own tongue as full and cause it to fall [into the fire] with the root mantra;
thereafter, one should worship the aforementioned mantra along with its *sāga* (concluding syllables) in the center.
Having done this, the practitioner of mantras should perform the oblation (*homa*) according to the specific ritual requirement.
Through milk mixed with ghee, eternal nourishment is attained;
through an oblation of ghee and guggulu, a full lifespan is certainly secured.
Thereafter, one desiring prosperity should offer oblations accompanied by ghee and milk;
then, one desiring a kingdom should offer bilva fruits smeared with the three [substances], which bestow excellent accomplishment.
Through the practice of oblation with fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees, one shall become possessed of clarified butter;
through oblation with excellent fuel-sticks, one obtains even more excellent results.
One attains all desires; this is indeed the truth and not otherwise.
By performing seven oblations of rice, one who seeks wealth obtains wealth.
Having directed one's effort toward the desired object, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with effort;
by means of milk alone, death is certainly conquered through the oblation in the Mṛtyuñjaya rite.
Through oblation with fuel-sticks of milk-exuding trees, one obtains a grove;
through oblation with excellent fuel-sticks, one obtains an excellent lotus in the water.
"One attains all desires; this is the truth and not otherwise.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the qualification for sacrifice, within the *Sāra* (Essence) of the *Mṛtyujit-Amṛteśa-vidhāna*, which is a compendium of all streams [of tradition].
The Lord said:
Now I shall explain initiation, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation:
the ten elements and subtle essences, mind, intellect, and ego.
One should thoroughly purify Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva— the eighteenth by name— within that very effect.
Prakṛti and Puruṣa, Nipati and Kāla,
Māyā, Vidyā, as well as Aiśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva.
The supreme teacher should correctly purify the principles (tattvas) in nine ways;
by thirty-six principles, by half of that, and by five, O Lord.
It should be performed with three or one [mantra] for the sake of supreme and inferior prosperity;
or else it may be performed with five kalās, or again with words (padas), or even as an initiation (dīkṣā).
It should be fashioned by means of the fifty letters, or by mantras, or likewise by the worlds; it may be made with all of these, or even with just one of them.
All [the disciples] together, by means of their collective power of manifestation according to their own nature,
should perform [the rites] with abundant resources, as prescribed by the supreme teachers.
The worship of Vāgīśī should be performed; one should place the bound soul (paśu) within her womb. Furthermore, there are the rites of conception, birth, empowerment, and likewise dissolution.
Enjoyment, the acquisition of karma, and thereafter expiation— these,
as well as the severing of the bonds, are prescribed to be performed with the root mantra.
The burning [of the enemy] should be performed with the Astra-mantra, while the state of being reduced to ashes is achieved by the Sthiti-mantra;
likewise, one should employ the root-mantra (mūla) for the severing of the crest-lock (śikhā-cheda) and for the fire-oblation (homa).
Having united [the disciple] with the supreme reality, one should cause him to take up his station;
for the sake of authority in the office of an ācārya, there is stability in the state that is both supreme and non-supreme.

One should know that the utterance *svadhā* belongs to the principle of Śiva; the initiation of knowledge (*vidyādīkṣā*) belongs to Sadāśiva; [the initiation] for the spiritual son (*putraka*) belongs to the supreme principle; and likewise, for the initiate bound by the rules (*samayin*), it belongs to Īśvara.

Thus has initiation been described in brief; it may be understood in detail from the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, in the section on the ritual of Mṛtyujid-Amṛtīśa. [This is the fourth chapter, the section on initiation.]
The Lord said:
I shall now explain the consecration (abhiṣeka), how and to whom it is bestowed;
it should be conferred upon the preceptor (ācārya) according to the ritual rule with eight jars.
These are declared to be the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), together with their consorts and their internal contents,
consisting of either five elements or three in the form of the principles (tattvas).
The knowledge of the Self, known as Śiva, is [imparted] by even a single person who is Śiva in essence,
for the sake of authority in the case of a teacher, and out of a desire for perfection in the case of a practitioner.
For one who has been consecrated and authorized should perform the mantra-sādhana;
being devoted to that vow, following its conduct, dedicated to it, and having it as his supreme goal.
Devoted to the practice of sacred observances, eating light food, with his senses restrained,
he should dwell in solitude in a holy field or within the precincts of a sacred shrine.
With a mind free from all attachments, the practitioner should begin the recitation;
first, the mantra-reciter, being well-composed, should recite one hundred thousand times.
By that, the common rites of the practitioner are accomplished;
indeed, by reciting it ten hundred thousand times, one attains terrestrial siddhi.
One will certainly attain the power of moving through the intermediate space after fifty thousand recitations;
the practitioner attains divine accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.
Just as the Goddess brings about accomplishment through the recitation of the *koṭikṛti* mantra,
so too does one become the all-pervading Śiva, capable of both restraint and grace.
He performs everything according to his will; he can sustain and intensely withdraw [the world].
He becomes certainly omnipresent, the knower of all, and omniscient.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the section on the ritual for the consecration and the means of accomplishment for Mṛtyujit-Amṛtīśa, within the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*.
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, I have heard that the Mṛtyujit [mantra] bestows both spiritual perfection and liberation;
now I wish to hear about that which is endowed with the threefold perfection.
The great-souled Amṛtīśa is the life-force within all living beings;
when he bestows success upon the world, he acts for the welfare of human beings.
It pacifies previously mentioned evils, destroys untimely death,
nourishes the body, and bestows auspicious peace and prosperity.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret:
how human beings, though submerged in the ocean of suffering, may cross over it.
Overcome by hundreds of untimely deaths, joined with old age and poverty, agitated by the fear of mental and physical ailments, and tormented by floods of sins.
O Dear One, just as all are liberated by the previously mentioned methods of slaying,
so too is there a threefold means— namely, the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
The King of Mantras performs extensively the gross rites of sacrifice, fire-oblation, recitation, and meditation along with water-offerings, as well as the mantras such as the *saṃpuṭa* and others.
Through the practice of the subtle wheel and by means of the sequence beginning with *kalā* and *nāda*,
one becomes the conqueror of death, attaining the supreme God who is the soul of all and the bestower of liberation.
O Dear One, when one is seized by Time and smitten by the fear of death, then,
for the sake of countering that, one should worship Amṛteśa.
One should worship the all-pervading Mṛtyujit, dedicating it to the name of whichever person one intends, according to the previously mentioned procedure with entirely white offerings.
Truthful speech, not false, swiftly delivers one from death;
it is joined with white sugar and sesame seeds soaked in ghee and milk.
In a circular sacrificial pit with three ridges, filled with fire and wood from auspicious trees,
one should perform oblations while reciting the name of the person protected, according to the ritual for great protection.
Even for one who has gone to the abode of Yama, there shall quickly arise great power;
or else, by means of oblations of sugar mixed with pure milk in the Mṛtyuñjaya rite, one becomes a conqueror of death swiftly— of this there is no doubt.
By performing a fire-oblation of fragrant ghee in a sacrificial pit made from the wood of a milk-tree, one should offer oblations;
Mṛtyujit will destroy death here, of this there is no doubt.
Or, a fire kindled with fuel from milk-exuding trees destroys fever in an instant;
likewise, sesame seeds, rice, honey, clarified butter, and milk [when offered] together [achieve the same].
This oblation of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) wards off all malevolent forces;
it is performed with pieces of guggulu incense, each three finger-breadths long and anointed with clarified butter in the measure of Indra.
O lady of excellent vows, nourishment quickly comes to one whose body is emaciated through the performance of oblations;
for when a man is seen to be weak and overwhelmed by disease, [this rite is performed].
But then, by encasing [the mantra] and reciting the name, one is liberated;
whatever mantra the wise man recites, he should encase it with Amṛtīśa.
O Goddess of the Gods, even one who is devoid of fortune and whose body is emaciated will quickly achieve success through this medicine that is encapsulated by mantra.

O Goddess, at that very moment it is given, and the powerful one attains nourishment. Having placed the life-force (jīva) within the center of the heart-lotus, enclosed between two moons, and infused with the letters of the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), death is swiftly overcome.
The knower of yoga should constantly meditate on the body as pervaded by the [syllable] *sā* (the letter *sa*);
he shall become liberated from all diseases—of this there is no doubt.
Seated upon a lotus in the midst of the Ocean of Milk, agitated by waves of nectar,
it is restrained by the upward and downward powers (ūrdhvādhara-śakti) and encapsulated by the letters of the sādhya.
He who meditates upon the true Self— whether his own or that of another—
as pure, both internal and external, with a form filled with the power of one's own nature (svadhā).
And with a mind free from agitation, one is liberated from all enjoyments;
[this occurs] when combined with yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron (kuṅkuma), and milk.
Upon a white lotus with eight petals, the object of the rite is placed in the center, restrained,
overcome by all diseases, and encircled by a lunar mandala.
One who exerts himself at the four corners, wielding the vajra and protected by the vajra, is liberated from all afflictions of disease; of this there is no doubt.
Upon a great sixteen-petaled lotus adorned with the sixteen vowels,
one should inscribe the name of the person to be accomplished by enclosing it between the first and last mantras.

Placing the *jīva* (the letter *ja*) at the end, situated within the *sāva* (the letter *sa*), and protected by the end of the *varṇānta* (the letter *kṣa*); having encapsulated it with the Lord of Nectar (*amṛtīśa*, the letter *ha*) around every syllable;
[one should place it] in the center and upon all the petals, situated within the lunar orb.
On the outside, however, the practitioner of mantra should draw a double lotus with the letters from *ka* to *sa* in sequence,
as before, obstructed by the syllable of the one to be subdued.
Following that, one should surround the external solar orb of the name of the person to be accomplished with the [seed] syllable,
encircling it on all sides within the city of Indra.
Having written the mantras with white sandalwood paste mixed with yellow pigment (rocanā) and milk, making them grey with powdered camphor;
The ritual procedure for great protection bestows happiness and good fortune;
O Great Goddess, one should worship this wheel with white flowers.
One should place it in the midst of honey with entirely white offerings;
by this very procedure, one becomes a conqueror of death within seven days.
One should not disclose the ritual for the protection of kings to others;
at the time of battle, it becomes a granter of boons that destroys the pride of enemies.
The knower of mantras should place each of the nine principles beginning with Śiva within the lunar orb,
from the center toward the east and ending in the northeast, by means of the Amṛtīśa mantra.
When one is overcome by hundreds of diseases and even by untimely deaths,
then one should worship with white offerings and with milk and ghee.
One attains peace through the performance of oblations with sesame seeds or with fuel-sticks of *kṣīra* trees;
having thus worshipped [the deity] within a water-pot (*kuṃbha*) provided with all medicinal herbs.
One should indeed perform the consecration upon the head with the sound of all auspicious chants, using pure water containing jasmine buds and filled with gems and water from a golden vessel.
There is no doubt that one who is afflicted by all diseases is liberated when they constantly meditate upon the supreme nectar, which is eternally arisen and free from ailment.
Having brought down the nectar from the supreme Śiva through the process of *prakṛti*,
it is poured into the vessel of the ninefold nectar, which is filled in nine ways.
Constantly agitated by fifty [deities], endowed with sixteen [fingers],
resting upon the foundation of infinity, and adorned with thirty-eight [ornaments].
Or, for the sake of accomplishment, he should remain uninterrupted by means of the five [nectars] until they are full;
thus, one who is devoted to meditation [attains] the nectar both internal and external.
The preceptor, intent upon the mantra and ever-abiding in a state of grace, should diligently sprinkle the disciple from the agitating flask held above his head.
In brief, there is no doubt that one transcends the difficult-to-cross cycle of existence;
[one attains] longevity, strength, fame, renown, fortitude, intelligence, glory, and prosperity.
The excellent kingdom of that king prospers in every way;
he who was afflicted by sorrow becomes free from sorrow, and he who was diseased becomes free from disease.
Even a barren woman obtains a son, and a maiden shall find a husband;
whatever desire she may long for, that very thing will certainly be hers.
O Goddess, out of a desire for your welfare, I have told you the greatness of the consecration and its prescribed ritual procedure, as well as the method of worship.
Through the ritual application of another scripture, one becomes worthy of all pacification rites.
Such is the gross procedure; now hear the subtle one as well.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Section on the Grounds, in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, within the ritual procedure for Mṛtyujit and Amṛteśa.
Īśvara said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the subtle and unsurpassed meditation:
the sixty seasons, the support of the vowels, the three lakhs, and the five voids.
It is joined with the twelve knots, endowed with the three powers,
traversed by the paths of the three abodes, and provided with the three channels.
O fair-hipped one, having understood that the body follows the paths of ten channels,
pervaded by seventy-two thousand and thirty-five million clusters of channels, and rendered [fragile] by fire and diseases;
By means of the supreme nectar of subtle meditation alone, when it has been brought forth,
the yogi nourishes either himself or another.
He becomes possessed of a divine body, free from all diseases; that which is his own true nature is self-realized, arising from the pervasion of one's own well-being.
The supreme power (parā-śakti) spoken of by oneself is established in her own state, while Śiva resides within her womb;
one should certainly perceive her in the central breath, between the prāṇa and apāna.
Then, O lady of excellent hips, having become that mantra situated there within the wheel, one should cause it to move by means of movement according to my own instruction.
Having formed that conceit, one should deposit it in the place of birth;
through the differentiation of states, one should apply it from that place to the *mūlādhāra*.
One should pierce by means of the application of the needle of sound through subtle yoga,
having pierced the sixteenfold foundation as well as the twelve knots.
Mounted upon the path of the central channel, one should pierce the supreme fixed point (dhruva).
Having then entered that, one becomes equal to it—the all-pervading Śiva.
Due to the abandonment of all ailments, it becomes partless through the power of *kṣobha*;
then, by that very same path, it is drawn back again into the interior of the heart.
As soon as it has entered there, the elixir obtained through meditation [is realized].
Having attained rest,
one should cause that entire nectar to flow from that place with force, and restrain it everywhere.
Indeed, by means of the differentiation of infinite channels,
one fills one's own city with the supreme, infinite nectar through the yoga of infinite meditation.
O Beloved, having likewise consumed everything internal and external through old age and death,
everything is thus filled by the subtle sound (sūkṣmanāda) arising from the conqueror of death (mṛtyujit).
Then, O Goddess, he attains success swiftly; this is the truth and not otherwise, having resorted to the place of birth, the throbbing middle digit.
Having established oneself as being situated therein, one should take refuge in the Fire of Time;
having gone there and grasped the consciousness, one should deposit that vigor right there.
From that vigor, the supreme power called Action (kriyā) arises as the intermediate state;
it is differentiated from above by consciousness (vijñāna), by the piercing of the knots (granthibheda), and by will (icchā).
Having relied upon the root-throb and then abandoned the two arms,
one should resort to that which is called Suṣumnā by means of the flow of the primary path.
Relying on that very [state], one should desist from the range of all the sense-faculties;
then, by means of higher consciousness, [the mind] gradually subsides completely.
Having gradually abandoned the causal deities beginning with Brahmā,
one reaches the power of sixty-fold intensity known as Kuṇḍalinī, the obstructress.
By the breaking of the knots such as Māyā, the fivefold group [of elements] beginning with the Heart (hṛdaya) is dissolved;
at the root of birth, known as Samaya, there is a knot arising from the bond of birth.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these five, abiding as the causes, are thus proclaimed at the beginning of the work.
The knot known as Indikā is that which is fixed on the wrong path and whose mind is intent upon it;
above that is Dīpikā, and above that indeed is Dadhi.
The knot called Nāda is the great knot, and beyond that is the knot of Śakti;
having pierced these twelve knots, one enters the supreme Śiva.
One should likewise pierce Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti, as well as the abode of Śiva.
The second void is at the navel called the "Birth," while the third is in the region of the heart,
and the fourth is in the center of the moon.
Now the six cakras, beginning with that called Nāda, are described.
The cakra of channels (nāḍīcakra) is called Janma; the excellent one called Māyā is at the navel;
the Yogicakra is situated in the heart; and the Bhedana is known to be located in the Tālu.
The wheel of differentiation is situated in the *bindu*, and that which is situated in the *nāda* is called the peaceful (*śānta*).
One should pierce all those previously mentioned [centers] with the spear of knowledge (*jñānaśūla*).
Having ascended the support known as birth, one should gradually press its root;
O lady of beautiful hips, listen further to the synonyms of that support.
The birthplace is indeed called Kūrma; there are five such sites called Kūrma.
Likewise, Matsyodara is said to be the Mūlādhāra.
Therefore, the knower of yoga should attain that mudrā known as khecarī;
for then, O Goddess, when the self is indeed sealed by the mudrā.
Then one should move upward through higher consciousness in successive stages,
piercing and breaking through until reaching the supreme station worshipped by the best of gods.
O Goddess, having reached that station, the Yoginī becomes one with the Equal Taste (samarasī);
having attained the partless state (niṣkala), she is the all-pervading Supreme Śiva.
Having thus become all-equal, motionless, and arisen from every direction,
thereupon proceeds the stainless power (śakti) which is devoid of objective characteristics (lakṣa).
Designated by mere will, consisting of knowledge and having the nature of action,
she is one, yet she exists through the differentiation of states and through his own differentiation.
Having filled [the space] with the Khecarī Mudrā up to the end of Śakti,
there is everywhere that which is void and stainless as long as the Moon has not arisen.
Pervaded by that which is grasped through meditative cultivation, transcending all states of existence,
supreme, all-pervading, the Highest Lord, incomparable, and free from affliction.
O fair-faced one, yogis who have ascended there become established;
that is the source of all the gods and powers, pervading everything on all sides.
The womb consists of Agni and Soma; from it everything proceeds.
The mantras that are composed therein become possessors of protection (trāṇavat).
It is the dissolution of all things and that very same supreme state;
from it, having agitated the supreme Śiva, creation proceeds.
Having attained the incomparable nectar by effortlessly agitating the *bindu*,
one obtains what is known as Candrodaya, the supreme and most excellent nectar.
One should contemplate there the infinite, surging waves of the nectar of bliss;
from that, having obtained the pure nectar, one should draw it forth by means of one's own power.
O lady of beautiful hips, one should analyze the causal factors by means of the middle path;
one should effect nourishment sequentially at each respective stage.
One should cause [the breath] to nourish the lower regions up to the station of Brahmā;
then, by means of the station of the place of birth, one should proceed into the fire of time.
Then, one should again contemplate it as being completely filled with perfect equanimity;
one should visualize the entire [body] as being fully saturated by the nectar of the *suṣumnā*.
Emerging from there through infinite channels and pores all around, it becomes pervasive, filling the sky with waves of nectar.
Established within the ocean of nectar, [it is] immersed in the ocean of nectar;
above that, indeed, is the pervasive Śiva, the flowing ocean of nectar.
Having thus become of one flavor, [one realizes] the nectar that faces in all directions,
the pervasive Śiva who is one's own self, consisting of will, knowledge, and action.
Having attained the state free from affliction, one should contemplate it through direct experience;
having reached the subtle station of Amṛteśa, one becomes immortal.
Then, having indeed become immortal, he is the conqueror of death; of this there is no doubt.
He is the conqueror of time, fortunate, and a hero; death does not afflict him.
I have revealed to you this subtle art of deceiving Time;
out of affection for your devotion, I have not disclosed it to anyone else but you.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the section on subtle meditation, in the *Amṛteśavidhāna*.
The Blessed One said:
Now, O beloved Mṛtyuñjaya, that which is eternal and transcendent is being described; having attained which, they do not return to the threefold cycle of worldly existence.
The yogi shines as all-pervading, all-seeing, and all-doing Śiva;
him I shall describe, for there exists nothing other than he.
That which is attained through identification with it indeed makes one ageless and immortal;
that which is spoken by the tongue of wisdom is eternal, and cannot be seen by the eye.
That which is not heard by the ears, nor does one smell with the nose;
nor does the tongue taste its flavor, nor does the sense of touch feel it.
It is not to be conceived by the mind; it is devoid of all colors and tastes, yet endowed with all colors and tastes, immeasurable, and beyond the reach of the senses.
O Goddess, having attained that [state], yogins indeed become free from old age and death,
through great practice and supreme detachment.
O beloved, through the abandonment of passion and hatred, the destruction of greed and delusion,
and the total relinquishing of intoxication and envy, they are freed from pride, arrogance, and darkness.

One obtains the eternal, constant, auspicious, supreme, and unsurpassed state. If it is obtained for even as long as the blink of an eye, from that moment on one is liberated and shall not undergo rebirth again.
One may attain [liberation] through the eightfold yoga, but never otherwise; constant detachment from cyclic existence is declared to be the supreme restraint (yama).
But cultivation in the supreme reality is said to be constant restraint,
having taken recourse to the middle breath within the interval between the paths of prāṇa and apāna.
One should take hold of the power of consciousness and that very seat situated therein;
having abandoned the gross state of the vital breaths and so forth, one follows the subtle alternative path.
But from that which the supreme vibration, subtler than the subtle, is obtained,
the mind does not stray from what is designated as prāṇāyāma.
Having abandoned that mental activity which experiences qualities such as sound, one should enter the supreme abode with one's own mind.
This is declared to be *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal), which severs the bonds of worldly existence;
it transcends the qualities (*guṇas*) through the intellect, reaching that which is beyond qualities, imperishable, and all-pervading.
Having meditated upon that which is to be meditated, which is self-realized, the wise know that to be meditation;
and they know dhāraṇā to be that by which the Supreme Self is held at all times.

That is declared to be *dhāraṇā*, which destroys the bondage of existence. Equanimity toward all beings, with the mind fixed upon the support [of the deity], is called *samādhi*; otherwise, it is merely worldly hypocrisy.

One who possesses an equal mind toward all beings, whether situated within oneself or others, in this world— thinking "I am Śiva, I am non-dual"— that is remembered as the supreme meditative absorption (samādhi).

The wise know that supreme concentration to be the true nature, which is to be experienced, whose form is consciousness, born of its own essence, self-perceived, and the very nature of reality itself.
Having carefully investigated the state [of reality] through both wisdom and discernment,
that which is thus the eternal form, they know that indeed to be true composure.
Thus, by means of the eightfold yoga, having beheld the supreme, eternal, and all-pervading Lord of Immortality abiding in His own nature, one transcends time.
O Goddess, he shall become a conqueror of death, and Time shall not be able to reckon him;
this is because of the abandonment of the thirty-six principles and the avoidance of the infinite worlds.
Indeed, beyond the eighty-one [phonemes] and the fifty letters, it is all-pervasive throughout all tantras; for it is the very life-force of them all.
Above the thirty-eight kalās, situated within all and in the center of all,
there is that of which no beginning, middle, or end can be found.
Having attained that incomparable, immeasurable [reality], nothing at all remains;
by that single, immeasurable one, the entire world is filled.
Knowing that, one is swiftly liberated from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra—
[that which is] eternally free from the three principles, perpetual, immovable, and constant.
Having seen through the divine path of yoga that which is liberated from all senses, the universal form, and free from affliction, one is not born again.
The nature of the Supreme Self, however, is described in all the scriptures as consciousness alone, which is the true form of the Self, entirely devoid of all limiting adjuncts.
O Goddess, it shall not become stainless as long as it has not been purified by Śakti;
one must purify both [the world] and oneself with the fire of knowledge through initiation.
Those who find nothing else and find the supreme state,
by that very fact they are worshippers of the Self and go to the supreme Śiva.
But when the Supreme Power, endowed with qualities such as omniscience and the rest,
is stainless and does not undergo modification from the feet upward through the process of expansion, [she remains as she is].

As long as the self is not stainless, it is said to be bound in the Śaiva [system]. That reality characterized by power (*śakti*), wherein the person, having fully restrained the collection of the senses, knows everything— past and future— is that very principle.
Wherever there may be desire or even where knowledge proceeds—
whether in the form of action or non-action— that very reality is characterized by power (śakti).
O Goddess, from the pervasive Self, whose nature is consciousness and who is auspicious,
there flows forth that most wonderful Power, which consists of marvelous bliss.
O Goddess, Śiva, the supreme cause, having expanded his self through qualities such as omniscience and being possessed of those attributes, is said to be "with manifestation" (sābhāsa).
He who is omniscient and completely satisfied, whose awakening is indeed unsurpassed,
who is independent and undecaying, and who possesses infinite power.
The possessor of power, endowed with qualities through the differentiation of those qualities, attains the qualified states;
through the distinctness of various divisions, he moves about here in manifold forms.
That which is called "all-appearance" is said to be "without appearance" (nirābhāsa). When there is neither "I" nor "another," such that it becomes without appearance—
that state is declared to be the supreme state of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Neither "I" exists nor does "another" exist, yet that which is to be meditated upon is found here;
knowledge has become absorbed in the state of bliss and attained a state of equal flavor.
One should apply the meditation above, not below, nor in the middle;
neither in front, nor behind, nor on either side.
One should not contemplate [the mark] as situated within the body, nor anywhere outside;
the focal point is not bound in space, nor should one direct the gaze downward.
There is no closing of the eyes at all, nor is there any binding of the gaze;
one should not cultivate support, lack of support, or even having support.
Having abandoned all things— including the sense organs, the elements, and [objects such as] sound, touch, and taste— one established in samādhi shall become identical with the Absolute (kevala).
That state is declared to be the supreme state of Śiva, the Supreme Self;
having attained that in the state of non-manifestation (nirābhāsa), one does not return.
Thus, by the power of his own meditation,
he who has cultivated the self shall become supremely peaceful, auspicious, and utterly stainless.
That single reality is everything, the auspicious Mṛtyujit;
and he is the supreme Amṛteśa, the third and most excellent state.
This has been declared to you, O Goddess of Gods; what else shall I tell you?
Thus, having known that everything is pervaded by the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyujit), one is liberated;
for at all times, O Dear One, the deception of Time has been described.
Thus, O Goddess, this threefold yoga known as the "deception of time," which is exceedingly difficult to attain, has been revealed to you by me.
By this practice of yoga, a person becomes a conqueror of death;
indeed, by this very yoga, out of a desire to benefit the world.
The yogi becomes a conqueror of death among all living beings at all times;
thus it is known as Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death), eternal, supreme, and fixed.
There is nothing higher than this; this truth has been declared:
that which is the nature of supreme nectar has been described by me as being threefold.
O Goddess, through the practice of that, a living being—whether for oneself or for another—becomes immortal, equal to the Lord, and a conqueror of death; of this there is no doubt.
In whatever manner and wherever he may remember [the deity],
in that very manner that yogi shall become a conqueror of time.

O Goddess, wherever one may be situated, by whatever vow, by whatever yoga, and by whatever distinction of disposition one attains perfection— that single [reality], when understood in its manifold ways, shall indeed bestow success.
Whether in dualism, non-dualism, or their mixture; whether in the Ekavīra or the Yāmala [systems], one shall become accomplished in every way and in all respects.
Just as in the world a wish-fulfilling gem bestows the fruit of whatever is desired,
so too does this king of mantras accomplish whatever purpose is intended.
The garland of the seven crores of mantras is supremely powerful;
however, those mantras that are devoid of meditative realization (bhāva) are powerless and obstructed.
Those who are devoid of even the mere color [of caste], those who have abandoned the arrival of the Guru,
those fallen and bereft of the tradition (āmnāya), and those hindered by being abandoned by the Āgama;
O Goddess, just as those rishis who have recited and performed sacrifices thousands of times do not achieve success—
being unsuccessful and devoid of all doubt— [so too is it with this mantra].
O Goddess of the Gods, they are not merely enclosed within the initial and final [syllables] by the syllable of the object of attainment (sādhya);
rather, they are ignited by this mantra, O Mistress of the Gods, which is illumined by Amṛtīśa.
O Goddess, those who have sacrificed and recited [mantras] shall undoubtedly achieve success without effort; you, when meditated upon, bestow everything—this word of mine is not false.
Thus, O beloved, this entire supreme secret has been narrated to you.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Deceiving Time," in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, within the ritual manual of Mṛtyujit Amṛtīśa.
The auspicious Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, I have heard the greatness of the Lord of Mantras;
now I wish to hear that which was spoken to me by Vidhu.
It bestows accomplishment through the ritual procedures of all scriptures and through the differentiation of internal states,
[applying] to the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Siddhānta, Saura, Vaiṣṇava, and Vaidika systems.

The Lord, who grants the accomplishment of one's desires through the practice of acting as one pleases, is indeed called Sureśāna; he brings forth the arising of the fruit of the fulfillment of all thoughts.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O beautiful one, to the truth; I shall tell you the ultimate reality.
According to the ritual procedure of Amṛtīśa, the conqueror of death has been described by me.
That alone, O Goddess, is the supreme, auspicious, subtle, and healthy state;
it is declared to be one's own true nature, all-pervading, eternal, and constant.
I do not speak of his form or color from the perspective of ultimate truth,
because the auspicious God is omnipresent and consists of all scriptures.
Pervasive among all mantras and bestowing the fruit of all goals, it is pure like crystal; that indeed is declared to be the white [syllable] and so forth.
Adorned by the method of the threefold universal consciousness, he reveals each [reality] accordingly;
thus, we are delighted by his very nature.
O Goddess of the gods, in that very same way, when applied according to all the Āgamas,
it bestows fruit upon all practitioners in every respect.
Therefore, shining like a wish-fulfilling gem within all the streams [of the body],
when meditated upon according to the distinction of one's disposition, it bestows the fruit of all desires.
Śiva, Sadāśiva, Bhairava, and Tuṃburu likewise—
the omnipresent Lord, who assumes the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
Since the Lord consists of knowledge and the object of knowledge exists in manifold ways, He is called the Eye,
for He is the protection for those who are restrained and bound.
Because he rescues one from death, he is awakened by the "Conqueror of Death" (Mṛtyujit);
because he bestows immortality, he is remembered as the "Lord of Immortality" (Amṛtīśa).
Thus, O Goddess, the omnipresent God, who possesses many forms like a jewel,
is worshipped by all with the desire for the fruit of their own spiritual accomplishments.
O Lord, you are the bestower of fruits upon all and the fulfiller of desired objects;
therefore, for a practitioner established in their spiritual discipline,
you shall grant whatever fruit corresponds to their particular disposition and the state of mind with which they engage.
O Supreme Goddess, when the practitioner constantly meditates upon [the Self] in the form of Sadāśiva, his body becomes that of Sadāśiva.
For this is common to all and brings benefit to everyone;
it is indeed the immediate Vāma, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna forms.
O fair-faced one, by means of this [mantra], the heart and other [limbs] should be assigned;
and by this very mantra, one should prepare one's own seat.
Resembling the moon and the arbuda mountain, appearing like a mass of clouds,
it had five faces, large eyes, ten arms, and three eyes.
He has a serpent as his sacred thread, is clothed in a garment of tiger skin,
sits in the bound lotus posture, and is seated upon a white lotus.
A trident, a blue lotus, an arrow, a rosary, and a mallet—these are in the right hands; hereafter, they are thus in the left hands.
From the eastern face, one should visualize the god as yellowish-green, bearing a shield, a mirror, a formidable bow, a citron, and a water-pot, with the crescent moon upon his crest;
the southern face is black, extremely fierce, with a mouth made terrifying by protruding fangs.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, he causes terror to the world;
his western face has the luster of snow and jasmine, while his left face has the radiance of a red lotus.

O Maheśānī, one should meditate upon the Lord of Devas as having an upward-facing countenance and possessing the luster of crystal; having thus meditated, one should worship Him according to the prescribed ritual.

One should worship [the faces], beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta, in their respective directions upon one's own body, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in a liṅga, or in water upon a lotus.
Having performed the placement of the heart and other limbs in the southeast and having worshipped them according to the rules, one will then achieve success without a doubt; I tell you this truth.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Authority of Sadāśiva," in the *Mṛtyujid-amṛtīśa-vidhāna*.
The Blessed One said:
Now I shall proclaim that which is distinguished by the Bhairava Āgamas,
resembling crushed collyrium in color and possessing the nature of the fire at the end of the aeon.
Five-faced, mounted upon a corpse, ten-armed, and terrifying;
appearing at the onset of night, most formidable, roaring with a fearsome sound.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, his eyes knitted in a frown,
clad in a lion’s skin, and adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, with a gaping mouth and a massive body,
his form was as vast as an elephant's trunk, and he bore the moon as his crest-ornament.
The god holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, carries a sword and a shield, wields a noose and a goad, and has hands that grant boons and fearlessness.
Having worshipped the great hero Bhairava, who holds a vajra in his hand and carries an axe as his weapon, one should then meditate upon her who has come into union with him.
Having a form like the fire of universal dissolution, with the luster of lac and the juice of the *siṃhaka* plant,
with hair standing erect, a massive body, and being most hideous and terrifying.
She has a large belly, five faces, and is adorned with three eyes;
she has claws for teeth, sunken eyes, and is decorated with a garland of severed heads.
The Lord, possessing arms as described by Bhairava and wielding the weapons of Bhairava, [beheld] her known as Icchāśakti, who rests upon the lap of Svacchandabhairava.
One should meditate upon her, renowned as Aghoreśvarī, who bears such a form.
That which has been proclaimed in all the tantras, yet remains concealed and not made manifest—
my intention regarding that is not perceived on earth, for it is difficult to find.

One should always perform sacrifice for the sake of pacification and nourishment in order to ward off diseases, planetary afflictions, and other such things, to prevent the destruction of lotus-like [beings], and for the protection of cows and Brahmins.
Alternatively, [one may meditate on the deity] possessing a luster equal to gold, kunda flowers, the moon, and pearls;
having a splendor like ten million moons, resembling a mass of crystal.
One should meditate upon that [deity] as red, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, like the hibiscus flower, or having the appearance of ten million suns.
Alternatively, one may worship the God who has the luster of a ruby, whose radiance is like that of emerald,
who assumes forms at will, and who bestows the accomplishment of all desires.
Whatever kind of color and sound the practitioner does not recollect,
such a form arises, which bestows auspicious accomplishment accordingly.
One should meditate upon the Lord situated in the center of a lotus and then worship Him according to the prescribed rite,
offering appropriate food, flowers, incense, and other articles.
She who is like milk, a goddess with a luster equal to the laughter of Hara,
resembling pure crystal, and as stainless as the kunda flower, the moon, and the moonlight.
The goddess has four arms and three eyes, adorned with a single discus;
she wears white garments and is embellished with white necklaces.
Seated upon a deer-skin throne, the goddess holds a vajra in her hand, possesses great strength,
carries a noose and a goad, and resounds with the ringing of a bell.
The abode of the God of gods is situated in the eastern direction, facing forward;
the practitioner who, with a disciplined mind, meditates upon it, quickly attains success.
Resplendent like ten million suns, with a brilliance like blazing fire,
resembling a heap of vermilion, having the form of lightning, and terrifying.
She has three eyes, a terrifying face, a stout body, and a large belly;
she has a protruding stomach and pendulous breasts, is mounted upon a corpse, and possesses great strength.
Adorned with a garland of skulls as her jewelry, with a tiger skin around her waist,
having an elephant hide as an upper garment, and decorated with a necklace of severed heads.
Shining with large, playful, and radiant tusks, illuminating the quarters and the sky,
she has four arms and one face, and she holds a sword and a shield.
One should meditate on her standing in the southern direction, bearing a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff;
she is dark-red, intensely radiant, fleshless, and has a distorted face.
She has eyes like dried-up hollows, one face, and four arms;
she is three-eyed, with a terrifying countenance, and adorned with necklaces of serpents.
With hair standing erect, possessing a massive body, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
her limbs bound with cords of sinew, her hips wrapped in human skin,
wearing a tiger-skin garment, and bearing a sword and a shield.
One should always visualize a pustule filled with entrails, blood, and flesh,
tearing apart the great intestines, located in the western direction.
Now, that which is established in the Kumbhīrāsana posture is described as follows:
it has the neck of a camel, the shoulders of an elephant, the ears of a horse, and the face of a rhinoceros.
Having the appearance of a snake's leg, with claws resembling vajra-weapons,
with a back like a tortoise and a tail like a fish— this is proclaimed to be the *kuṃbhīra* [mudrā].
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, resembling an autumnal cloud,
she has three eyes and one face, and is adorned with blue garments.
Mounted upon the back of a lion, with bow and arrow raised in her hands,
the Great Goddess likewise holds a spear in one hand and a lotus in the other.
In the northern direction, one should meditate upon the Goddess of the Gods, who bestows fruits when worshipped:
Siddhāraktā, Śuṣkā, and likewise Utpalamālinī.
O Dear One, these [goddesses] who are fierce and terrifying stand in the four cardinal directions;
one should assign the messengers (dūtīs) to the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast up to the northeast at the ends of the quarters.
Kālī, Karālī, and likewise Mahākālī—
the goddess renowned as Bhadrakālī abides in her divine form.
But what about these two-armed goddesses seated upon lotus-thrones,
and these servants at the gateway who carry knives and wear shaven heads?
Krodhana, Vṛttaka, Karṣaṇa, and Gajānana—
these two-armed deities have distorted faces and hold swords and shields in their hands.
For the purpose of pacification, however, all [deities] are white, or their form [is determined] according to the distinction of the ritual action.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the consecration of a king.
By means of the yoga of enclosing with mantras, one should write the name in the center;
O Dear One, one should worship that deity Bhairava, the Lord of Nectar (Amṛteśa).
Just as the goddesses were previously appointed by him upon the petals in that same manner, so now the messengers are likewise appointed with the root mantra; what shall they do?
Outside the lotus, one should draw a very white moon-maṇḍala;
outside that, a square marked with the signs of the [four] faces.
Having written [the mantra] with yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron, milk, and sugar, one should drink it; for the sake of pacification, one should worship it with entirely white offerings.
Just as with forms, food offerings, voracious [beings], Bali, and liquors;
mixed with white sandalwood, grey with powdered camphor,
along with unbroken rice, sesame seeds, and white sugar.
If one should offer oblations of *tuyantī* mixed with clarified butter and milk,
there will quickly be great peace, even if one has been seized by death.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Section on the Southern Face," in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, within the ritual manual for Mṛtyujit and Amṛteśa.
The Blessed One said:
Now I shall proclaim the unsurpassed Uttara-tantra;
one should perform sacrifice with this mantra, which brings about the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments.
O Goddess, for the sake of pacifying all calamities, one should [worship] the god Tumburu in the center of the previously mentioned eight-petaled lotus mandala.
One should thus fashion the faces with the body of Sadāśiva, who has ten arms, is the lord of the gods, possesses five faces, and has three eyes.
He has a crescent moon upon his head, is seated upon a lotus throne,
is as white as snow, the kunda flower, or the moon, and possesses a splendor like that of the sun.
He has a serpent as his sacred thread, is adorned with all ornaments,
is endowed with every kind of jewelry, and wears a tiger skin around his waist.
The god is clad in an elephant hide, mounted upon a bull, and possesses great strength;
he bears a sword and a shield, and is adorned with a chisel and a *kaṃdala* fruit.
The god holds a noose and a goad, and carries a discus, an axe, and a measuring line;
his hands grant boons and fearlessness, and he is the destroyer of all sins.
The goddesses are stationed in the four cardinal directions, beginning with the east, as well as the messengers (dūtīs);
likewise, the servants (kiṅkaras) are in the intermediate directions, beginning with the southeast, at the locations of the gates.
Jambhanī, Mohanī, Subhagā, and Durbhagā as the last—these, O Dear One, are declared to be the female messengers (dūtīs), while the male servants (kiṅkaras) are as follows; listen!
One should establish Krodhana, Nṛttaka, and the mighty Gajakarṇa;
then one should place Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī on the left and right sides.
Immediately thereafter, one should place the hook (aṅkuśa) and the illusion (māyā) below and above;
all these [syllables] should always be joined with the root mantra.
The goddesses are indeed white, red, yellow, and black;
they have four faces, four arms, and three eyes, and they hold a ṭaṅka and a kandalī.
Those holding staffs and those with threads in their hands shine forth surrounding the pretas;
and the goddess Jayā, as well as Vijayā, are four-armed and possess beautiful complexions.
The goddess has four faces and three eyes, and she holds a bow and arrows;
she carries a sword and a shield, and she stands upon a lion.
Jayantī has the complexion of the interior of a lotus, four garments, and four arms.
The Goddess holds a spear and a bell; she carries a shield and a short sword. Mounted upon a horse, the Great Goddess is adorned with all ornaments.
And Ajitā has four faces, is black in color, and possesses great strength;
she has four arms and three eyes, and likewise holds a noose and a goad.
Holding jewel-studded bowls and maces in their hands, they were well-seated upon divine thrones;
bearing golden vessels, they were adorned with golden ornaments.
The worshippers stationed in their own respective directions, when meditated upon, bestow the fruit of accomplishment;
the messengers (dūtīs) assume those same forms, but are adorned with only a single face.
They have two arms and three eyes, and are adorned with a severed head and a razor;
their seats are likewise a fish, a tortoise, a crocodile, and a frog.
The servants have swords in their hands, possess two arms, and carry shields;
they have one face and three eyes, with frowning brows and squinting glances.
The auspicious Gāyatrī, meditated upon according to the distinctions of colors such as white and so forth, bestows accomplishment; she is red in color and adorned with a single face.
Seated upon a lotus throne in the *vatra-padmāsana* posture, her eyes were closed in meditation;
Sāvitrī’s eyes were absorbed in meditation through their white radiance.
Likewise, the goddess Māyā was four-armed, with limbs of a dark complexion.
From the pair of hands joined in the form of a casket, which encloses the great cloth,
[he arises as] the Lord, who has the form of Bhairava and holds a noose and a goad.

He holds a skull-bowl and a khaṭvāṅga staff, is greedy for fat, blood, and flesh, and is like the ocean of milk to the sound [of his laughter]; he possesses the auspicious Śakti who is the supporting earth.
One should employ [these] for the purpose of a seat, which accomplishes the goal of all pacification;
or, O Goddess, all these, when very white, bring about peace.
They should be meditated upon as red, yellow, and black according to the distinction of the ritual action;
likewise, one should perform worship when they bestow the fruit of accomplishment.
Now I shall fully describe another, the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja) of great power;
one should write the name in the middle of the union between the beginning and the end.
In this manner, the wise one should meditate upon the goddesses and the female messengers (dūtīs) according to the previously mentioned procedure—
whether in the center, on the petals, in the sub-petals, or elsewhere, in every respect.
