For the sake of one's own abundant peace, as well as that of others, appropriate food offerings (naivedya) should be presented and the rite of pacification (śāntikarman) should be performed here.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before in a sacrificial pit kindled with excellent fuel, using sesame seeds, rice, honey, clarified butter, milk, and sugar.
Great peace shall arise; let not one speak a falsehood.
For the performance of all protective rites, the goddesses who grant excellent accomplishment should be employed.
Or one may worship the Goddess arranged in a row, with the god Tuṃburu in the center;
the practitioner who is self-controlled attains all auspiciousness.
Or by employing it for another, one conquers food without a doubt.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, concerning the ritual of Mṛtyujit-Amṛtīśa, in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, within the section on the *Uttaratantra*.
The Blessed One said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the demonstration of the Kula tradition—
the sacrificial offering, the fire oblation, and the recitation— which, when performed, enables one to attain everything.
In the center of the lotus, Bhairava, previously mentioned, is to be fully worshipped;
indeed, the eight goddesses abide by their very nature upon the petals located in the directions starting from the east.
And the forms, weapons, and vehicles of the deities beginning with Brahmā:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
O beloved, just as a farmer holds the seeds of his field within his granary, so do these [energies] hold the form of the world within their power;
they sustain it during dissolution and create it here once again.
And just as farmers sow seeds at the proper time for the sake of fruit, so too [does He act] out of a desire to emit the Brahma-kalpa for the sake of its fruition.
At the beginning of the eon and at its end, those who act for the welfare of the world pervade it;
therefore, with every effort, for the sake of peace and out of a desire for benefit, [one should practice].
Those desiring success should perform sacrifices,
offer oblations, and practice meditation using all types of seeds, sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets, or auspicious bilva fruits.
With flowers that are highly praised, or with other excellent fruits, I offer oblations;
[these are] the goddesses who bestow all accomplishments and grant the fruit of all desires.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the section on the Kulāmnāya, within the *Mṛtyuñjidadṛtīśavidhāna* from the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*.
Īśvara said:
Thus indeed has been declared the Kaulika ritual of the King of Mantras as enjoined by the rule; now I shall further proclaim another procedure which bestows its fruit.
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, four-armed, with eyes as large as lotus petals,
resembling the color of an *atasī* flower, with one face and two eyes,
adorned with all ornaments and holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
The god, wearing divine garments, adorned with celestial flowers,
and embellished by a shimmering network of pearls, rubies, and tiny bells.
One should always remember Him as wearing divine earrings and risen [in the sky],
or else as seated upon the king of birds, brilliantly white and beautiful to the mind.
Having three faces with gentle countenances, adorned with boars and lions,
and endowed with six arms, he is equipped with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate on [the consort] upon his lap, possessing a beautiful touch, bearing the same colors and weapons as he,
equal to the God of Gods in loveliness and splendor, and facing him directly.
One should worship the goddesses stationed in the cardinal directions and the limbs in the intermediate directions;
one should likewise worship Jayā, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and Māyā in the intermediate points.
I meditate upon the Goddess who holds a noose and a goad, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness,
who stands facing the Lord, and who bears the form and color of Śrī.
One should [visualize] the limbs of the god as being similar [to his], bearing weapons of eight colors;
or else, the god with eight arms, beautifully radiant and yellow in color.
The god seated upon a ram, naked, with a liṅga upon his head, holding a horned vessel (? and a staff in his hand.
I constantly worship the one in the form of a child who is indeed sporting with women;
one should place the goddesses, naked and beautiful, in the four directions.
She who assumes the forms of Karpūrī, Candanī, Kastūrī, and likewise Kuṅkumī— the Goddess who bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of one's desires.
What is the use of saying more here? One should always remember [the deity] as the consumer of all, with a multitude of many faces and likewise with many arms.
Or one should meditate upon the Lord on his bed during the wedding ceremony, joined with Lakṣmī,
or as Narasiṃha alone, or as Vārāha.
Or one may meditate on the face of Kapila, or even on the unmanifest and partless;
by whatever means or through whatever distinction of mental state one might recollect [the Lord].
"He attains identity with that"—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, I shall describe that which consists of light, by means of which men may attain perfection.
Having a form resembling a red lotus, with a radiance equal to liquid lac,
possessing a hue like a mass of vermilion, and a brilliance similar to a ruby.
Resembling the juice of safflower, with the luster of a pomegranate flower,
like the fire at the end of an aeon, he has a single face with two eyes,
four arms, and is the Great-Souled One whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should hold a vajra with one hand and a lotus with the other;
he is mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses and wears a snake as a sacred thread.
Wearing red garlands and garments, with red flower-garlands and unguents;
or else, the eight-armed deity equipped with the weapons of the world-protectors.
One should always worship [the deity] in the center of the lotus, mounted upon a horse, possessing three faces, a terrible countenance, three eyes, and a distorted mien.
One should worship the Heart, Head, Crest-lock, Armor, Eyes, and Weapon;
one should worship the Deity in the central lotus, and the eight planets in the second.
In the third [circle], however, one should worship the constellations in groups of three;
having worshipped the triad at the tips of the petals, one should then sacrifice to the world-protectors (lokapālas).
In the fifth lotus-position, one should worship the eight weapons;
they may be depicted either alone, well-erected, or with two arms, accompanied by rays of light.
Or [he may be] the very embodiment of Viśvakarman, the creator of the universe and the progenitor of the world;
the great-souled one with four arms, bearing a chisel and a book.
One should visualize him being praised by gods, siddhas, and gandharvas, holding a rosary in his left hand and a thread in his right hand with reverence.
One should worship on dry land, in water, or indeed on mountain peaks;
or wherever the mind finds pleasure, for it bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of one's desires.
One should meditate upon him who is as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon; who has three faces and the form of Rudra; and who, in the form of Sadāśiva, is mounted upon a bull.
The great-souled Lord has four arms; he is endowed with a trident and the gesture of fearlessness, holding a mātuluṅga fruit and a rosary of beads.
Alternatively, one should meditate on the Lord who has many arms and resides within the navel,
the God who bears Umā as half [of his body], and Viṣṇu likewise bearing her as half [of his body].
One should meditate upon the marriage ceremony or worship one who is standing nearby;
[one should visualize] Brahmā, four-faced, gentle, red in color, and with beautiful eyes.
With a long beard, possessing great luster, mounted upon a swan, and four-armed;
holding a staff and a rosary in his hands, and bestowing both a water-pot.
Endowed with the four Vedas, he bestows the fruit of all accomplishments;
the Buddha is seated upon a lotus throne, with long arms and ears reaching down to his shoulders.
Lotus-eyed and marked with the lotus, adorned with jewels, he is the benefactor of the world;
the great yogi remains absorbed in samādhi, his hands granting boons and fearlessness.
The god who wears a rosary, holds a lotus in his hand, and possesses beautiful eyes—having meditated upon him in this way, he should be worshipped; he bestows the fruit of liberation even upon women.
O beautiful one, what is the use of saying much more here repeatedly?
[Therein dwell] Kārttikeya, Kāma, Soma, Sūrya, and Vināyaka.
One should worship all the world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as other divine beings, in the Gāruḍa, the Bhūtatantra, and the rules for the employment of speech.
[It is taught] by the Nyāya, Arhatas, and Sāṃkhyas, and in every way by the Vaidikas;
[it is found] in the Yāmala, the Ekavīra, and the Navaka, according to their respective divisions.
To the one who bears half of Umā, and likewise to the one who bears half of Viṣṇu;
to the goddesses situated near him, or the one known as Durgā, the dweller of the Vindhya mountains;
and to Caṇḍikā and the others, Śuṣkā and the others—you are Maheśvara himself.
Or [one may worship] in a form previously consecrated, or in one fashioned by sages and men,
and in all weapons and in all seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) everywhere.
O lady of excellent vows, by this mantra, even the infinite powers within the Pātāla mantras and tantras, as well as those released by the lords of the Nāgas, are subdued.
When worshipped according to the prescribed rite, they bestow the fruit of all accomplishments;
this is not false, O blessed lady, for my word is true and never untrue.
The God is common to all, bestowing the fruit of all accomplishments;
for He is remembered as the very life-force of all castes.
The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and the worship (pūjana) are performed with the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) and the arghya vessel;
when the external [deities] are stationed, they are worshipped once, as are the forms of the moon and the sun.
In the cremation rite by fire, one must not entertain any doubt regarding the placement of mantras (nyāsa), meditations (dhyāna), and the ritual vehicles (vāhana), because these are common to all.
Confusion shall not arise; therefore, one should abandon all doubt.
[The mantra] residing in the body is to be recited once, while that in the vessel of offerings is to be recited once.
In the case of mental recitation, the placement [of the mantra] upon the hands is performed once;
when standing outside, one should worship it once in the forms of the moon and the sun.
In the fire-oblation one should sacrifice once; in the whispered recitation, once; and in the water-offering, one should sacrifice once.
In every instance, one should worship the Supreme Lord once and only once.

O lady of excellent vows, for this king of mantras, the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other such hardships, as well as the yoga of concentration (dhāraṇā) and mudrās, are of no use at all.
It must be accomplished through resolute efforts; otherwise, it will not succeed at all for the preeminent practitioner in his kingdom and for the expansion of the realm, provided there is no flaw.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the section on all vidyās, in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, within the ritual procedure for Mṛtyujit-Amṛtīśa.
The Goddess said:
If this supreme mantra, which has been described as being of the nature of the Devas,
belongs to all the gods and goddesses in every respect;
For this king of mantras is the supreme heart that bestows all accomplishments; what need is there for other chief mantras, whether worshipped or recited? Speak your desire.
The Blessed One said:
O Great Goddess, O sinless one, I have been well asked by you;
I shall fully explain that which is the supreme, eternal essence.
This was in the form of Śakti, incomparable and free from affliction.
O Goddess, Śiva— who is all-pervading, pure, immeasurable, and beyond the senses— desiring to create by his will, becomes the embodiment of action through his power of knowledge.
For he, O Goddess of gods, is the first, the omniscient, the all-pervading Śiva;
he is the God who is everything, whose self is everything, and the initiator of the primordial creation.
Then, indeed, the emanation of mantras was fashioned by Śiva, the Supreme Self,
in various ways according to distinct classifications.
Just so, O Goddess of gods, the Supreme is everything and the self of all;
the Lord of Mantras is common to all and the expressive signifier of everything.
For at that time, he is indeed the self-form of all, untainted;
for innumerable millions of mantras, both manifest and unmanifest, abide within him.
All of them grant success when they are bound by that beginning and end;
by reciting them through this method of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*), they bestow the fruit of accomplishment.
O fair-hipped one, out of affection for you, half of this supreme secret and truth has been revealed; it must not be disclosed to just anyone.
For this [mantra] bestows perfect accomplishment when kept secret, whereas if it is made public, it destroys accomplishment.
O Goddess of the Gods, he is the first, the omniscient, auspicious in every way;
he is the all-encompassing God, the Lord who performs the primordial creation.
That very creation of mantras, which is indeed Śiva, the Supreme Self,
is fashioned in various ways and, abiding as the Goddess, sends forth [her commands].
O Goddess of gods, each and every thing is thus the supreme essence of all;
therefore, this oral tradition of the lineage must be kept strictly secret.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Universal Authority," in the *Mṛtyujid-amṛtīśa-vidhāna*.
The Blessed One said:
Hereafter, I shall explain how to prepare the incense that provides all forms of protection, which is impelled by the Lord of Mantras, the Great Fierce One, and which destroys demons.
If this, consecrated seven times with mantras, is given as a protection against demons,
one who constantly wears it upon the head is liberated from all defects.
Indeed, for the sake of destroying all the Daityas, Brahmā himself performed an *abhicāra* rite against all the gods,
including Śiva, according to the prescribed method.
Indeed, the mustard seeds are always said to protect and guard [the practitioner] from all sides,
since all the rākṣasas have already been struck down by the opening of the door.
O Goddess, when I proclaimed you as the world-renowned slayer of Rākṣasas,
you were appointed by the best of the gods to destroy their enemies and eliminate the wicked for the sake of success in all battles against the Daityas.
O Goddess, when their purpose was not accomplished, that [mantra] became known on earth as Asiddhārthaka; it removes the pride of beings with wicked minds.
When all beings are terrified on every side by fear,
one should offer oblations into the fire with the name-marked [mantra] according to the procedure for the rite of *nairājana*, O Dear One.
When the practitioner, with a mind full of wrath, is intent upon protection within the fire,
that is known as the Nairājana rite, which is supreme and brings about all prosperity.
The planet becomes powerful according to the difference in the Yugas;
it is renowned as white when bestowing everything, and red when establishing sovereignty.
The yellow [complexion] is declared to be the protector and the destroyer of enemies;
however, throughout all four ages, in the second [age], both yellow and black [complexions] are present everywhere.
O beloved, two forms known as Rāja-sarṣapa and Gaura are beneficial;
yet when one is seized by the power of death, one is pursued from all sides by black calamities.
At that time, however, having prepared an offering mixed with ghee, white sugar, cow's milk, and sesame seeds, one should perform the oblation; this bestows peace upon all.
One should properly offer as an oblation the excellent black mustard seeds mixed with sesame; this is auspicious and bestows all peace.
O Goddess, when this very [mantra] has been consecrated and placed into someone’s hand, incomparable good fortune will undoubtedly be won.
Having consecrated it seven times with this mantra, the knower of mantras should cause it to be placed upon the head of whomever [he intends]; that person is liberated from all defects.
Having thus consecrated incense, flowers, garments, or medicinal herbs,
or having consecrated an ointment, a drink, or food;
For it is said that those who cause harm do not harm the one to whom [the offering] is given;
therefore, for the protection of that person of disciplined mind, one should scatter [the offerings] in every direction.
Whether by day or by night, whether asleep or even awake,
that man remains as a protector among all beings.
Thus have I revealed this method for the protection of kings;
out of affection for you, I have disclosed this excellent secret which bestows all accomplishments.
He who acts as a preceptor for kings, queens, and their sons among the twice-born is one who bestows grace upon all.
Whether he be a knower of mantras or a practitioner, he is in every way a lord worthy of worship with constant honors, garments, wives, and various extensive offerings.
Just as the word *svāhā*, when joined with the meaning of a mantra, bestows fruit in a fire-oblation (*homa*),
so too is one who knows the mantras always consecrated for all ritual undertakings.
It shall rightly bestow fruits, granting all powers and auspiciousness,
just as nectar is for the Nagas and as the Svadhā offering is for the ancestors.

The utterance of "namaskāra" is praised for the gods, while "vauṣaṭ" is recommended for pacification; likewise, for those who know mantras, the constant offering of gifts and excellent honor is supreme.
It becomes fruit-bearing in these [times], bestowing all accomplishments;
the mantras abide in the power of knowledge, and that knowledge abides in the mind.
That mind, when honored and satisfied, always becomes characterized by sattva;
for one who is constantly established in sattva, glory and prosperity ever increase therein.
When the qualities of rajas and tamas are destroyed and sattva arises, mantras always quickly bestow success, because they become exceedingly pure.
Therefore, with every effort, this command of the Supreme Lord must be diligently observed;
then accomplishment and liberation will not be far off.
One should not bestow the supreme ritual upon one who has been initiated by another;
one should bestow it upon one's own disciple once he has been initiated, and never otherwise, O beloved.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, in the section on the ritual of Mṛtyuñjaya-Amṛtīśa.
The Goddess said:
The God of gods has spoken this most wonderful secret concerning the God who consists of all the Agamas— the Sole Hero of great power.
The secret doctrine is proclaimed as being composed of the left and right Siddhāntas, distinguished by the three divisions, and joined with the Vaiṣṇava and other systems.
For this Śiva is composed of all the gods, the conqueror of death, and all-pervading;
he is to be worshipped through many traditions according to the distinctions of one's inner disposition.
Through various ritual services, it bestows various fruits of accomplishment;
now I wish to hear that which resides within the heart of self-restraint.
Apart from you, indeed, no one capable of cutting through this doubt can be found;
for everything concerning the various distinct modes of conduct has been declared by the Lord.
How is this common conduct, proclaimed everywhere, to be practiced? And how is it that by means of a single mantra, all [deities], when worshipped, grant their accomplishments?
Through seeds, syllable-combinations (kūṭas), as well as clusters (piṇḍas) and garland-mantras in their manifold forms,
and by means of the distinction between the signified and the signifier, it bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
How may a man become worthy of worship by means of a single mantra?
For all the gods here attain their respective positions through the power of their own [mantras].
O Supreme Lord, out of compassion for the welfare of human beings,
you have arrived during the Kali age so that men who are deluded by suffering may attain perfection.
Tormented by the fire of poverty, beset by the fear of old age and death,
devoted solely to drinking, cruel, and devoid of austerity and truth.
Violent, malicious, and intent on harming, they are excluded from pure conduct;
they are joined by yoginīs, śākinīs, ḍākinīs, ḍāmarikās, and others.
"O Maheśvara, tell me how those who are sealed by spirits, yakṣas, and epilepsy may attain success when they are free from them. Śrī Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O illustrious lady! I shall speak according to what you have asked, O Great Goddess, for the Kali age will be most difficult.
For that purpose, I have revealed to you the ultimate reality;
the supreme goal, by its very nature, is the all-facing Mṛtyujit.

One who desires the attainment of liberation should worship according to the distinction of their inner disposition; whatever conduct has been taught by me in various scriptures for each particular case, that is to be followed.
In the case of the Srotas-tantra, the rites for sacrifice and oblation must likewise be performed with specific details;
otherwise, O Goddess, they will never succeed in a general manner.
However, there is no restriction regarding these three types that grant all perfections;
whether dualistic, non-dualistic, or mixed, when practiced, they indeed bestow success.
Because the omnipresent deity is like a multiform gem,
when worshipped according to the desire of the practitioner, he certainly bestows accomplishment.
Since the omnipresent Lord is all-pervading, immanent within everything,
and the bestower of both worldly success and liberation, castes have no ultimate reality.
Therefore, O Goddess, everything should always be worshipped according to the distinctions of one's inner disposition.
I shall explain its sacrifice; it may be performed according to one's desire.
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or at a crossroads;
in a forest or a delightful grove, according to the requirements of place and time.
In this dwelling of one's own, which is free from all thorns, devoid of wicked beings, characterized by meritorious dharma, and which has cast out evil conduct;
Where the citizens are never seen to be intent on censure,
and where those wicked ones see everything everywhere as being mixed with auspicious things.
In that [house], the great mantra should be worshipped with songs devoid of [worldly] melodies;
the sacrifice should be performed in the home by the teachers who perceive reality.
It must be kept strictly secret, especially during rites for pacification;
however, at the time of initiation, a mandala should indeed be constructed wherever it may be.
For the sake of pacification and nourishment, one must certainly perform the sacrifice with great care and secrecy;
for in this world, those who cause harm are seen to attain success through violence.
The pinning down of mantras, as well as their piercing, deluding, striking,
paralyzing, and immobilizing.

Furthermore, by means of their various limbs, wicked ministers indeed cause the creation of enemies, the very state of being an adversary, and total ruin; thus, in these ten ways, do those who would do harm fall [into calamity].
Therefore, with every effort,
one should have the food-offering, the fire-sacrifice, and likewise the recitation of mantras performed in one's own home, well-concealed above the sanctuary.
The fruit is exceedingly excellent, well-guarded, and eternally victorious over death;
it resides in the mandala, on the sacrificial ground, and in the pitcher, yet it is not perceived by the mind.
Likewise, a fire sacrifice performed atop a palace especially bestows peace and nourishment;
O Goddess of Gods, there should be no hesitation here, for through hesitation one goes to the Raurava hell.
One should recognize that thief as one who causes the loss of accomplishment, [even] while performing a sacrifice or a fire-oblation right there which bestows the fruit of all attainments.
O Goddess, he too would not be qualified in the Pārameśvara Tantra;
rather, he should be one who knows all things, a knower of reality, and a teacher of the paths.
Thus, he who understands pervasion according to the distinction between the higher and the lower shall become a direct liberator, Śiva himself, the supreme cause.
But he who performs initiation and other rites without knowing the reality of Śiva is like one who leads the blind with a blind man; both shall fall into the abyss.
Having led both himself and the disciple into the peril of hell,
how could the illustrious Ācārya, who knows reality and is all-pervading,
perform ritual acts until he has become the most excellent knower of reality?
Just as one who knows mantras and knows the yoga of Brahman [perceives] the other as one's own self,
so long as the mantra is not pure, how can there be accomplishment?
O Goddess, it becomes stainless, and the mantras residing therein become perfectly pure;
born from that and equal to it, they bestow all accomplishments.
And by the command of Śiva and Śakti, there arises the auspicious emergence of mantras;
since mantras bestow fruit everywhere, they are remembered as Śiva himself.
Therefore, all [gurus] consist of Śiva and constantly bestow grace;
and since Śiva himself exists in the form of the teacher, they are traditionally held to be the givers of the fruit.
O Goddess, as long as one has not obtained a true knower of reality, whether it be a guru or even a practitioner, so long will [the practice] not yield fruit; I tell you this truth.
Otherwise, it would not bestow the fruit of being a teacher while joined with worldly enjoyments;
therefore, one who knows reality is the most excellent in all actions at all times.
Therefore, any creature who has been initiated by him becomes auspicious even if he were a slayer of a Brahmin;
and in whatever place one may reside, whoever performs this rite in such a manner [attains the same].
By whatever means of practice, by whatever distinction of existence,
or by way of the general, the particular, or the Kaulika, O lady of good vows.
If the Lord Sadāśiva is pleased, he swiftly accomplishes each of those goals,
whether on a square or a circular altar measuring one cubit or even more.
Everything is accomplished by the will of the Teacher through the realization of pervasion;
by means of the nature of the power of action, Kauṇḍilyā effects the piercing of pervasion.
Having realized that the *kuṇḍa* is all-pervasive, the Guru becomes the giver of everything;
for as long as one does not find the pervasiveness of both the *kuṇḍa* and the self, [one cannot bestow all].
One who knows the six paths of the fetters—both the goal to be attained and the bound soul—plays like a child; how then could there be any task remaining for him?
Furthermore, he who knows the self to have the nature of Śiva and Śakti—
he is the bestower of all fruits, the supreme, the creator, the omnipresent Śiva.
The fire consisting of the power of knowledge, through the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader,
becomes the Guru— the creator of all, the bestower of liberation, and the giver of fruits.
The Guru who performs the sacrifice transcending the six paths is Śiva,
the protector of all, who has arisen from the ocean of Māyā like the moon.
He who practices yoga while remaining in the midst of the path without discernment is not able to liberate either another or even himself.
One attains no accomplishment whatsoever and is incapable of performing any action;
indeed, bondage is traditionally defined as impurity (mala) arising from the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
In this expansion, the māyīya, āṇava, and karmic [impurities] are the causes of bondage;
the bound soul (paśu) is not present therein, for the Guru alone has the power to grant liberation.
The fetters situated within the middle path perpetually sprout from the self;
knowing that which is beyond them as supreme, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Who might not be a giver of liberation? Who always attains perfection? Who would be a donor, a minister, and who is capable in action, O Dear One?
That supreme state is auspicious in every respect; having known it, one should become absorbed in it.
The Guru, who makes himself heard, finds it through measurement, weighing, and direct perception.
He becomes as skillful as an artisan, creating various forms;
yet he does not become a bestower of liberation, nor does he grant the fruit of spiritual accomplishment.
Therefore, all should be regarded as equal to Śiva by those who know the truth.
The teacher (ācārya) is traditionally said to be of three kinds: the practitioner of ritual action (kārmin), the man of knowledge (jñānin), and likewise the yogin.
O Goddess of the gods, both ritual action and yoga bestow the fruit of knowledge.
Knowledge and action appear as distinct divisions through the practice of yoga;
therefore, one who possesses knowledge shall always be foremost among the noble ones.
Taking refuge in Śiva and established in Śiva, impelled by the power of Śiva,
he— remaining as the very form of Śiva— creates this entire universe.
One who is endowed with will, knowledge, and action, and is proficient in the principle of Śiva,
acts according to the will of Śiva, being established as pervaded by knowledge.
Inconceivable indeed is the power of mantra, born from the mouth of the Supreme Lord;
by relying upon the power of Śiva, the knower performs whatever he wills through it.
Each of those things is accomplished through the power of Śiva’s energy;
the mantras facing him alone produce immediate, perceptible results.
Śiva, the supreme cause, performs all rites— such as pacification and others— against poisons, spirits, and planetary influences, in an instant.
O Dear One, he who, endowed with the power of the yoga of knowledge,
awakens that [disciple] through the majesty of the power of mantra, shall bestow initiation.
By destroying the bonds of impurity, one attains the supreme state;
thus, through the power of Śiva-Śakti, Śakti should unite [the soul] with the Yojana.
The mantras directed toward that very [deity] produce immediate results,
performing rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) against poisons, malevolent spirits, planetary influences, and the like.
This is observed as the sign for him alone, and not for anyone else—
in the Gāruḍatantra, the Bhūtatantra, the Vāmasrotas, and the Dakṣiṇasrotas.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the fierce period of Dhārā, this rite yields manifest results even for this man who is extremely impure and bound by Māyā.
This initiation, whose nature consists of ritual action and knowledge, bestows liberation upon one who is attached to worldly enjoyment and possessed of desire through [the performance of] karma.
But she who has her mind fixed on that Supreme Power, the Avadhūtī whose nature is knowledge—
she is designated as "Action" (Kriyā), for she does not abide within the path of action.
The power of yoga and the power of knowledge are celebrated in all the scriptures;
that power belongs to the Supreme Lord Śiva, the remover of all inauspiciousness.
She brings about bondage and liberation for men, yet she is not independent by her own nature;
by this very measure, Śiva is the auspicious bestower of all.
The lineage of gurus beginning with Śiva consists of many tens of millions of Rudras,
established through the path of authoritative instruction in an unbroken succession.
O Goddess, since the knowledge of Śiva is remembered by all as the authoritative tradition (āgama),
it extends from Brahmā down to the very end, and is endowed with the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti).
Thus, the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of power;
the possessor of power performs all actions—of this there is no doubt.
Rites such as pacification and others are indeed rites; they do not otherwise exist.
Devoid of power, they are not accomplished even in hundreds of millions of aeons.
Even with thousands of crores of recitations and hundreds of thousands of extensive fire-offerings,
one should therefore practice the knowledge of Śiva with every possible effort.
Then all these rites will indeed succeed, for they do not otherwise;
at that time, the Guru performs the rites such as those for pacification (śāntika) and so forth.
In sacrifice, fire-offering, and recitation, as well as in the sequence of drawing [mandalas],
if a calamity should arise, one should begin the sacrifice exactly as prescribed.
When one who has accumulated those two types of provisions under the name of the person for whom the rite is intended performs the sacrifice, peace arises for that person.

One should perform a fire offering with sesame seeds, milk, and ghee, together with white sugar, while reciting the name of the person for whom it is intended; thus, that person shall attain great peace.
With a well-concentrated mind, one should perform a fire sacrifice using fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees smeared with milk;
by reciting the name of whichever person [is intended], that person's peace will certainly be attained.

If one performs a fire offering with *sumana* flowers mixed with clarified butter while uttering someone's name, that person will quickly attain peace; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Those desiring prosperity, having offered *śrīphala* fruits, obtain abundant fortune;
through an oblation of ghee and *guggulu*, there arises eternal nourishment.
If one recites the name of the person to be protected while encasing it within the *mṛtyujit* mantra,
death shall not afflict either oneself or another.
One should place [the name] within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus;
when the name is enclosed by the letters of the sādhya, it shall thereafter be the conqueror of death.
One should place the limbs upon the petals according to the divisions starting from the southeast (āgneya);
outside that, one should draw a lotus complete with sixteen petals.
Then, one should fill [the lotus] starting from the east with the sixteen vowels;
outside of that, one should place a lotus endowed with thirty-two petals.
In the same sequence from *ka* to *sa*, extending from the east to the northeast,
all the letters of the target name are situated in red within the three wheels.
Among all of them, one should indeed restrain the consciousness of the person to be accomplished;
one should place the life-force, situated in the center, within the pericarp of the name.
At the end of the breath, one should visualize the living soul situated between the end of the breath and its color;
externally, however, one should fashion a beautiful, perfectly complete mandala.
Outside of that, however, is the city of Indra, pierced by eyes and thunderbolts;
having inscribed this wheel upon a birch leaf, O fair-faced one.
On a very white, flawless, and smooth surface, [one should write] with yellow pigment (rocanā) or saffron mixed with Malaya sandalwood juice,
greyed with powdered camphor.
Having wrapped it with black thread and new cotton,
one should place it within honey, mixed with fragrant ghee.
Having placed [the image] within an earthen vessel, one should worship it with white flowers,
with milk-rice mixed with ghee, and likewise with various kinds of edible offerings.
Having fumigated with refined incense, one should worship with offerings consisting of sacred ash;
then, one should worship eight jars externally, starting from the east.

[One should prepare] a beautiful vessel— made of gold, silver, copper, or clay— which is filled with water containing gems, endowed with all medicinal herbs, and overflowing with white sandalwood, camphor, and excellent incense.
Having worshipped the auspicious and praiseworthy Akālamūla tree, which is endowed with all the characteristic marks,
one should then worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) among them in due order.
Having given them the command of Śiva, one should then worship them at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight, for the sake of accomplishing the supreme protection.
When seven nights have passed, the person becomes a conqueror of death—
liberated from all diseases and freed from all defects.
One shall be liberated from all diseases and from all fevers, without a doubt;
one shall be abandoned by all suffering and freed from calamities.
And the man remains upon the ground like a hooded serpent,
O Goddess, provided that the practitioner has no other mind and is solely devoted to that [practice].
Devoted to recitation and burnt offerings, peaceful, he dwells in this place;
endowed with courage and fortitude, he is possessed of compassion and courtesy.
When seven nights have passed, he should forcibly bring back even one who is dead,
along with cattle, land, gold, garments, armlets, bracelets, and other such items.
He is to be worshipped with supreme devotion, especially for the sake of peace and nourishment;
for he, the Guru, is indeed Śiva himself, manifest as the mantra.
O auspicious lady, by merely being worshipped by him, all mantras become fruit-bearing;
this is undoubtedly true and not otherwise.
Otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment and what has been performed would indeed be useless;
furthermore, the teacher and the intense activity of the one to be accomplished would arise.
Therefore, with every effort, the knower of mantras should worship the Guru;
when worshipped, the mantras become bestowers of the fruits of all accomplishments.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Section on Pervasion, within the *Mṛtyujid-amṛtīśa-vidhāna* of the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*.
The Blessed One said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja) of great power;
O Dear One, one should arrange the name from the center as before, ending at the life-thread (jīvā).
Then, at the end of the vital breath (prāṇa), having placed the final letter situated within the other letters,
one should then place the last [letter] on the outside, and the middle one on the outside of that.
Then, one should place the first [syllable] outside that, upon the pericarp;
the vowels should be joined to the filaments, and one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) on the petals.
On the outside, however, a flask (kalaśa) should be drawn, with a skull situated in its center;
one devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, and worship should honor it according to the previously mentioned ritual.
It accomplishes whatever is intended in no time at all; of this there is no doubt.
This wheel bestows all peace and grants nourishment and good fortune.
It bestows longevity and vigor, is meritorious, destroys diseases such as fever,
and brings victory to kings who are terrified by the kingdoms of their enemies.
This protection, which destroys all calamities, should indeed be employed for the wives of kings, for their sons, and for Brahmins and others in every respect.
O Dear One, one should write the name separated by intervening syllables using the *paṇḍityā* [method];
one should then place the original root mantra joined with the *vauṣaṭ* exclamation.
One should worship extensively as before upon a white and auspicious noose;
at that very moment, one is released from diseases, even if already seized by death.

One should beautifully write the mantra joined with *vauṣaṭ* and the [seed] syllable of one's caste in the eight directions upon a lovely birch-bark surface; in the center, however, the name is written as before.
Combined with the words of protection, that [should be placed] outside on a lunar disc;
it consists of the syllable at the end of the mantra, which is nectar and endowed with the sixteen digits (kalās).
Having filled the circle of the *tāḍi* tree, one should place a lotus on the outside;
and outside of that, the Moon and the Sun situated in the city of Indra,
one should draw with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), milk, and sugar.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual while remaining at the end of the eastern lineage,
she is indeed declared to be "Rājaraktā," the destroyer of all calamities.
For the ritual procedure of protecting the king, one should perform a fire oblation (homa) consisting of milk,
combined with white sugar and fragrant ghee.
When men are seized by Time and overtaken by death, peace will certainly be attained through sesame seeds offered into a fire fueled by the wood of milk-exuding trees.
Having performed the sacrifice as before, the mandala should be constructed according to the instructions;
when provided with the necessary materials, it becomes the destroyer of death.
Death is swiftly overcome by the power of this mantra;
that very [mantra] should be written on birch bark together with white sugar.
One should draw [the design] with cow's bile mixed with milk and saffron;
then, one should place it well-concealed within a golden jar smeared with honey.
Above that, however, one should meditate upon a second [vessel], beautiful and filled with milk, pouring forth nectar; having thus visualized it, one should install it for the sake of nourishment.
By practicing for seven nights, a person becomes a conqueror of death;
though his body may have been wasted away, it becomes full like the moon at the end of the fortnight.
O son of Sūrya, he is not subject to the power of death; know this to be the truth and not a false word.
This name, which is to be accomplished by recitation, is accompanied by protective syllables.
One should join the object of accomplishment in the center as before, having rendered it immortal;
then, one should indeed envelop that very self again with the water-mantra (vāruṇa).
One should encircle that with a remaining portion of the *kalā* and then with a complete [portion] on the outside;
then, one should place Indra on the outside within the range of the two [gates] in the four directions.
It should be joined at the edge of that mandala, placed between the hollowed palms;
protected by the Lord of Nectar (Amṛteśa), it shall never cause fear to him.
The Yoginī becomes [invulnerable] to spirits, protectors, Rākṣasas, and those who cause harm;
likewise, all Brahma-Rākṣasas, as well as Ḍākinīs and Ḍāmarikas, [are likewise overcome].
For the sake of their protection during the beautiful rites of sacrifice,
one should place them upon a lotus, having written their names inside a water-pot.
Then, one should draw the Puṣṭikamala with its face turned downwards as before;

O Maheśānī, having meditated upon and recited [the mantra] which bestows the fruits of both supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mukti),
one should worship the Goddess of the gods after having performed sacrifice to her residing within the water-pot.
In the auspicious sacrifice previously described, according to the aforementioned procedure,
one should worship her situated within the pitcher by means of meditative concentration as before.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should perform the consecration as before;
by its power, Mahālakṣmī bestows sovereignty or whatever is desired.
Whether it be the accomplishments of the earth or the atmosphere, or even the auspicious, divine power of the Lord— whatever desired object one may long for, He, being well-pleased, bestows it.
Longevity, strength, fame, renown, intellect, luster, prosperity, and physical form—
all these increase for that person in whose house she is worshipped.
O Dear One, whoever is consecrated, or for whomever one performs this rite, shall obtain everything previously mentioned: peace, nourishment, and happiness.
But for whomsoever the Goddess, depicted on a cloth, is worshipped in his house according to the previously mentioned procedure, she bestows everything upon him.
What need is there for much speaking here? Just as all deer flee from a lion, so do all wicked faults flee by the thousands.
What need is there for other groups of mantras or for the propitiation of deities,
when this Goddess of the lords of gods is meditated upon, recited, and worshipped?
At the time of battle, one should meditate upon the sword-blade creeper standing firm;
it bestows victory, brings [all] under control, and becomes the destroyer of the enemy's pride.
Always to be employed at the front of battle, it shall destroy the pride of enemies;
one will certainly attain victory through the grace of the Goddess of Gods.
Whether afflicted by hundreds of diseases, tormented by suffering and grief,
smeared with every malady, or oppressed by magical spells and *khārkhoda* poisons;
Indeed, those deceptive practices such as mantras, yantras, meditations, recitations, fire-offerings,
powders, ointments, collyriums, and so forth;
Wherever enemies shall act, whether against women or even against men,
if they are honored by this ritual procedure, it shall become their *pratyaṅgirā* (counter-spell).
Whoever, having taken refuge in the Supreme Goddess, worships her with devotion,
shall not be seen by wicked men who delight in sinful conduct.
It should be worshipped while being well-concealed from those who have attained mantra-perfection, as well as from rogues, violators of sacred commitments, and thorns;
thus protected, it becomes a bestower of success.
Whether in sacrifice, fire-offering, recitation, ritual gesture, or through the yoga of meditation,
he who meditates upon the Goddess while she remains well-concealed shall become a possessor of good fortune.
For many wicked people desire to destroy their happiness;
they have abandoned the good fortune of others and are themselves tormented by misfortune.
They always perceive [the practitioner] during sacrifice, fire-oblation, and the rites of recitation and meditation;
they produce great obstacles. Therefore, the procedure must be kept secret. That [Goddess] should be worshipped by the wise practitioner according to the distinctions of inner disposition.
Furthermore, when the Sovereign of the Gods is worshipped according to the "Single Hero" (ekavīra) procedure,
the Supreme Goddess, being well-pleased, grants all desires.
In the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava Siddhāntas, the Supreme Goddess is worshipped distinctly;
according to the differences in the minds of her devotees, she bestows the fruits [of their practice].
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem in this world bestows the fruits of whatever is desired,
so too does this Great Lakṣmī bestow the fruits of all desires.
Gods, asuras, and humans; nāgas, gandharvas, and kinnaras; sages, apsarases, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
The spirits, vetālas, yoginīs, mothers, and likewise the guhyakas;
the ḍāvis, ḍāmarikās, goddesses, sisters, and likewise the messengers.
Therein dwell all the lords of yoga and those perfected in yoga in every way;
by means of great glory and grace, they are all perfected beings who bestow perfection.
Mahālakṣmī is the embodiment of all accomplishments and possesses great power;
she is the bestower of boons upon the devoted practitioners who have taken refuge in her.
For there is indeed nothing else superior to her that bestows happiness upon the world;
nor are the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, nor even those who are omniscient and supreme.
O Goddess, O Beloved, all these men attain accomplishment, and not otherwise;
or one who seeks liberation should likewise worship the Solitary Heroine as before.
Alternatively, one should install the all-pervading Lord, endowed with His powers and accompanied by all the necessary ritual materials, within a delightful temple.
Having established [the deity] according to the prescribed rite through the union of power and the possessor of power,
whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of other births [is destroyed].
At that very moment, O Goddess, he does not see [the world], like a mass of cotton in a fire;
merely by being enveloped, he is established as the Lord of Gods, or even initiated.
He uplifts his entire lineage— ten ancestors and ten descendants—
as far as the temple, the linga, the image, or the painted walls.
As well as the mineral ores of stone, banners or flagstaffs,
oceans, rivers, Mount Meru, the moon, the sun, and the earth.
He experiences that number of those atoms for such a duration;
having experienced [the fruits] in the principle of Sadāśiva through that enjoyment, he shall attain nirvāṇa.
Just as the Sindhu river, upon reaching the ocean, becomes one with it in its essence,
so too the bound soul (paśu), having attained the state of Śiva, is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
Indeed, one shall obtain this fruit of consecration; there is no doubt in this matter—provided it is not performed for uninitiated kings, their sons, or members of the twice-born classes.
Or else, O Goddess, due to indolence regarding enjoyments, or because of the defects of karma and obstacles,
neither sacrifice was performed, nor penance practiced, nor meditation undertaken, nor [the deity] installed.
O Goddess, for those who have died through acts causing loss of caste and are established in hell due to many causes, including children, women, and the elderly;

For the sake of elevating the deceased and for the purpose of initiation, the Supreme Lord—the primordial Lord of Gods—should be worshipped; or else, a specific ritual action should be performed therein.
O Goddess, it must certainly be made of silver, or else similar [to it], measuring twelve finger-breadths;
or it may be made of cow-dung, O Goddess, purified by bathing with *kuśa* grass.

In that case, initiation alone brings about the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) by means of pervasion; it leads [the soul] equally [to all levels], and one should unite the individual soul (aṇu) with that [level] and cast it into the fire by means of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Through the *yojanī* [rite], she shall then attain union with the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).
At the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*), one should worship the God, or perform a sacrifice (*yajet*) with the mantra "iti" for the fulfillment of desires.
Likewise, O Goddess, the Guru should perform the installation upon a cremated body in a cemetery,
using the previously mentioned collections of materials and according to the previously mentioned procedure.
O Goddess, one should visualize the previously described terrifying form, endowed with two śaktis, whether four or eight [arms], as seen in the prior meditation.
One obtains the fruit previously described; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Mṛtyujit-Amṛtīśa," in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*.
The Goddess said:
The God of gods, desiring the welfare of living beings,
has declared this supreme ritual of Amṛteśa, which brings about all forms of protection.
Now I wish to hear the doubt residing in my heart:
why do mothers always cast their gaze upon living beings?
Innumerable goddesses endowed with immeasurable power are praised;
yet even these most powerful yoginīs are afflicted by a flaw in their shadow.
They were exceedingly powerful, fierce, merciless, fearless, and firm; they were harmful to all living beings, and especially to children.
No number can be found for them; therefore, tell me the means regarding that which is the fruit in the form of a shadow, as well as the deception of the falling glance.
O Lord, how many such shadows are traditionally said to always exist? What is the fear regarding the casting of their gaze, and how indeed is it averted?
"O wielder of the trident, speak all of this in brief out of your grace.
The Blessed One replied:
Listen, for I shall fully describe the characteristics of Chāyā;
indeed, the Mothers are immeasurable, infinite, and exceedingly powerful.
And there are spirits of various forms, infinite and of great power—
yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others who are harmful and deceitful.
No number exists for them, as they are established in millions of divisions;
I shall speak in brief that by which children may be liberated.
Women, men, royal consorts, and their sons likewise abandon [their lives] by force, being devoted to sacrifices and vows.
With bodies armored by mantras and endowed with great measurable strength,
they appeared by the thousands in various royal lineages in a former kalpa.
Everywhere there are violent and cruel beings, ever intent on killing;
they are all attendants of Bhairava, always prepared for sacrifice.
By that power, all those who are strong, their vigor augmented by it,
being observers of great vows, gratify [the deity] with the offering of great sacrificial animals.
He assumed a form as Mahābhairava, with Svacchanda as his vehicle,
for the purpose of slaying the Daityas and establishing the gods.
When the gods, headed by Indra,
were constantly oppressed by the Ādityas and driven away by the Daityas, I was then praised by the deities.
For the sake of their welfare, when Brahmā and others offered various hymns of praise,
I assumed the form of Mahābhairava by my own free will.
For the purpose of routing the Daityas and establishing the gods,
the Mothers were created by me out of compassion for that end.
Having defeated the pride of their enemies with those [weapons] and having achieved their purpose,
they came into my presence and, fearing the threat of destruction, made their request.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, you have indeed been gratified by us;
therefore, by the grace of the gratified God of gods, let that which is to be done be performed.
When they said, "Do it, O God," those mighty ones, who were invincible due to the granting of boons, were then set in motion by me as they desired;
thus they all became exactly as they had been created by me in the past.
From that time forward, the entire world— both stationary and moving, including gods, humans, and animals— was all oppressed by them after being attacked.
Moreover, powerful beings in heaven seek to slay the gods;
likewise, those who are strong on earth seek to slay human beings from all sides.
And various beings of the animal realm likewise seek to kill others;
they are said to be innumerable, possessing immeasurable and fierce strength.
Furthermore, I was praised by the gods, Prajāpati, and Purandara;
at that time, all beings, even those who were more powerful, were overcome by me.
The mothers of fearsome form, having become terrified with fear, approached my presence; all of them, obedient to my command, arrived while performing their duties.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, being enraged, he brought down many millions of mantras into the houses of the Mothers for the purpose of their destruction.

By the power of Śiva and Śakti, all the infinite mantra-deities and others, whose nature is contemplation and protection, have been authorized by me; terrified by the fear of the power of Vidyā, they have come into my presence.
Then, acting under the power of my command, they were dispersed by me upon the lands and in the waters, throughout the intermediate directions and the voids.
Some desire to return, others likewise desire to eat, while I, however, desire pleasure;
these desires are born of wind and also of bile.
Those born of phlegm, those born of the humors combined, and other beings of various forms— I have declared them all to be powerful, yet they remain subject to my control.
O beloved, they indeed hear my words, which are joined with mantras, mudrās, and various meditations, and which pierce through the five streams.
Then everyone, terrified with fear, fled in the sixteen directions;
with all their many treasures, they sought to kill that man as if he were a beast.
One who is of evil conduct, evil-souled, impure, and the lowest of men—
by not honoring his mother and father and by avoiding their service— he consumes their essence in vain.
Excessive attachment to women, and especially persistent indulgence,
as well as sexual intercourse at the wrong time, through delusion, out of fear, or due to agitation.
Those who have abandoned the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), those who engage in sexual intercourse during the twilight hours,
and those who indulge in eating, study, sleep, or sexual union during the twilight periods;
Those who lust after the wives of their gurus and others whom they should revere, and those powerful men who by force violate women against their will— [they go to hell].
Likewise, others who speak untruths, those who commit treason against their lord,
those who perform inauspicious acts, men who do not speak when they ought to, those who engage in sin, and those who are hostile toward Mādhava;
By these and other such causes, human beings are seized by the grahas;
and women are likewise afflicted due to immoral conduct and the eating of impure or forbidden food.
Likewise, due to hatred toward both [parents] and because of infidelity toward their husband,
as well as other unmentioned faults, they defile [the lineage] and seal it [with their own corruption].
The gnashing of teeth by children, as well as keeping vigil at night,
and being terrified at night, are all corrupted by evil shadows.
A woman in her menses, female messengers, and those who are most sinful or impure at that time;
likewise, one who is insane, fleeing, terrified, trembling, or corrupted by faults [should not be employed].
Then, weeping and crying out with disheveled hair,
the women were defiled by the touch of wicked Pukkasa-Caṇḍālas,
as well as by the touch of the corpse, by entering [the house], and by the touch of those staying there.
Furthermore, due to association with the wicked, one follows their conduct;
likewise, there is impurity and so forth, because of being defiled even by various forms of untouchability.
Whether it be a wicked woman or a wicked man, having bathed, one should cause [the image] to be placed in the shadow for children,
kings, their queens, and ascetics.
And through a gap in the shadow, the Bhūtas and the Mātṛs, who are exceedingly powerful, cast their glances; for these destroyers seek out even the slightest openings.
Fierce-eyed and intent on slaying the foolish,
these most sinful and ill-behaved beings afflict others with fevers and other ailments.
Then those enemies—mad, evil-minded, of wicked conduct, and deeply distressed;
hungry, envious, and arrogant in their hostility—[approached].
These and many other portents, terrifying in their sudden appearance,
are seen by all means among the ignorant as well as those previously mentioned.
Therefore, having recognized a favorable glance, one should act for one's own welfare;
one should not delay even for a moment, for there is no such thing as a small deed [that does not yield results].
Faults do not afflict one while they are merely present; rather, having resided there, they cause affliction.
Therefore, one should not delay at that time, but should act with complete decisiveness.

There, he should cause [the purification] to be performed with many highly praised medicinal herbs accompanied by auspicious rites, or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with mantras.
The bath, which generates good fortune and removes all defects and fears,
is performed by the preceptor with mantra-consecrated jars as previously prescribed.
It is always and immediately beneficial for the aforementioned children in every respect;
it is meritorious, instantly producing the highest good, bestowing nourishment, granting luster, and auspicious.
For when the infinite Mothers residing there are present, O dear one,
and desire to strike [the practitioner], then one should immediately worship the Mahāmātrīs.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers.
By worshipping these seven Mothers, one becomes auspicious;
they are proclaimed to be the sources of the entire circle of Mothers.
As soon as they have been honored with various kinds of offerings,
the entire assembly of Mothers becomes satisfied at that very moment.
These seven are proclaimed as the foremost among all mothers;
they are worshipped with various kinds of white, yellow, red, and black flowers.
With milk-rice, *kṛsara*, fish, and various kinds of linctuses,
and with the four types of meat, as well as with voracious and powerful [beasts].
By worshipping the garlands, immediate welfare shall arise;
therefore, through the sacrifice of offering, the deities become the recipients of the qualities.
They become satisfied everywhere and shall indeed attain all that is most auspicious;
thirty thousand crores [of beings] were created by me from my own thumb.
If any man is obstructed or overcome by those terrible Vināyakas whose minds are ablaze with fire, [he shall be freed].
Therein, one should worship the presiding deity Vighneśa Vināyaka with the ritual services (upacāra) of another tantra and through the yoga of meditation.
One should cause gold, jewels, vehicles, and seeds to be given;
everything should be caused to be given to everyone in its own respective form.
He is liberated from obstacles and his goal is accomplished at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
If a man is seized by fierce and powerful spirits or ghosts, then one should employ Bhūteśvara according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Where living beings are certainly oppressed by various Rākṣasas,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, having performed a sacrifice there, shall attain all prosperity.
When a man is excessively afflicted by innumerable yakṣas anywhere,
then indeed, having quickly performed the Śravaṇa sacrifice, he shall attain liberation.
Likewise, if the two divine [deities] belonging to the eight wombs are in conflict anywhere,
then one should perform the Bhairava sacrifice and shall attain the highest good.
A large, voracious inner offering (antarbali) should be given to all;
then, one desiring spiritual welfare should offer the outer offering (bāhyabali) in the sacred field.
The forest-dweller should offer another oblation with buffaloes and the like, as well as with various animal skins; he should cause this offering to be presented to all.
On a riverbank, in a cremation ground, in a forest, or in a circle of Mothers;
at dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight.
They should be given at the *balistha* [offerings], by which they become satisfied;
for one should cause water mixed with food to be offered to them in great abundance.
By this, may they all be satisfied— those who bestow the fruit of every highest good—
and may they never prove false toward you, O auspicious lady, but protect you like a mother;
[granting] memory, intelligence, victory, growth, physical form, longevity, fame, and happiness.
Because it bestows strength upon all who have lost it, it is known as *bali*.
Thus, everything should be performed with the *mṛtyujit* [mantra], which grants all accomplishments.
For children seized by the Skanda-grahas who are afflicted in body,
as well as for women overcome by the Rati-grahas, [this] may sometimes be effective.
Then, by worshipping Kārttikeya according to the previously mentioned procedure,
those infant-seizing spirits (śiśugraha) such as Skanda and others will certainly and swiftly release them.
In whichever family this [lineage] is sealed or, in some cases, pinned down, one should not perform sacrifices in that family; thus one is liberated from all defects.
But half of that entire secret has been revealed by me in this tantra, according to the ritual procedure of Amṛteśa for all beings.
In all these, the commonality that conquers death has been made manifest;
it is the secret heart of all, unproclaimed and most wonderful.
I have not been questioned by anyone, nor has this secret— the oral tradition that brings about all supreme well-being— been told by me to anyone.

Those practitioners who, through devotion, truly worship with effort, are liberated from all sufferings; this word is true, not false. By this alone is one's own task accomplished, which is the eradication of all suffering.
One should cause [the rites] to be performed for one's devotees, one's own sons, and one's own wives;
likewise for one's disciples and devotees, but one should not employ them otherwise.
Because it is the preceptor of all stages of life and because of his constant sovereignty over kings,
as well as their sons and wives, one who desires their welfare must always perform service for him.
One should always perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites for the sake of peace;
and when the mouth has been rinsed, one should always apply a white sandalwood tilaka.
At that time, for the removal of defects, one should perform the rite seven times with mantras;
likewise, at the time of bathing, one should apply a tilaka mark with white ashes.
To whomsoever an anointed flower or betel leaf is given,
the violent do not harm them here in this world.
The knower of mantras, having consecrated the food with this mantra,
eats between the two moons and attains immortality.
The king remains on earth liberated from all diseases;
furthermore, during his times of play, he [rides] upon elephants and buffaloes.
For protection during all forms of missile-play (*astra-krīḍā*), one should worship the *kalaśa*;
indeed, for the sake of play, for victory, and for protection against harmful beings and the like,
since many wicked ones seek to kill even kings.
Therefore, one should employ this auspicious protection that brings about all prosperity;
then, while the king is asleep, one should worship the jar of sleep.
One should worship [the vessel] made of silver, joined with medicinal herbs, and smeared with sandalwood and agallochum;
or, filled with milk or water, one should worship it and recite the Mṛtyujit mantra.
With entirely white offerings— flowers, incense, water for the guest, and milk-rice—
one should worship Mahānidrā, who resides within the book and causes the delusion of the world.
O King, one should contemplate that the command-tooth was set in motion by the God of Gods for the sake of happiness at night and for the sake of digesting food and so forth during the day.
Then the entire night passes away in sleep,
along with yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others, as well as evil dreams and the Mothers.
Freed from fears and the sufferings of terror, he may abide in happiness,
even among the world-protectors, the celestial weapons, and the kings, for the sake of protection.
When the jar has been worshipped, the wise and supreme teacher should constantly perform worship with water-offerings (argha), flowers, and other articles for that [deity].
"The Blessed Lord Śiva has said that one obtains all that was mentioned previously;
and during all auspicious occasions, one should always worship Amṛteśa."
Since one who can assume any form at will (kāmarūpī) should perform sacrifice,
he shall thereby obtain all desires for the sake of protecting the subjects and for the abundance of grain and crops among the settled farmers.
Therefore, for the sake of protecting his wives, for the prosperity of his kingdom,
and for the sake of victory among kings, he should worship [the deity] in the form of Indra.
For the protection of cows, land, and Brahmins, as well as for himself and his kinsmen,
he should perform extensive worship with sacrifice in his own home on the day of Mahānavamī.
One attains the previously mentioned excellence, as well as longevity, health, and prosperity;
therefore, the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) should be performed with diligence for the sake of attaining perfection.
One attains mastery over the weapon and, when it is employed, reaps its fruit;
this occurs when the king has been seized by the power of death at the time of dawn.
Or his sons and others may take the property from the place marked by the fatal signs,
among all the Brahmins and others, as well as among the citizens and the people of the countryside.
Rice flour and other grains [should be offered] with water containing fruits and roots during famines,
epidemics, and other such calamities, as well as during extraordinary portents.
Then, for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, the Nairājana rite should be performed;
having performed the sacrifice as before, he should consecrate [the king] with the water-pot.

The preceptor, free from hesitation, should perform this auspicious rite in a secluded place at night, accompanied by the sounds of "Victory! and "Auspicious Day!", as well as Vedic hymns, auspicious rites, and svastika symbols.
Consecrate the king and cause many offerings for the fulfillment of goals to be made;
O Dear One, one should offer oblations marked with his name according to the ritual of *nairājana*.
With a mind full of wrath toward the fire, the practitioner,
intent on protection, should sprinkle many goats for the sake of satisfying the host of spirits.
Or, having discerned an auspicious omen through the flight of birds,
O Indra, perform a sacrifice in the north-western direction (Śivavāruṇī), which bestows all perfections upon one who has set out.
Then, O Goddess, one should perform the domestic sacrifice (gṛhayāga) according to the previously mentioned procedure for seven days, which grants success through abundant oblations.
The king shall obtain unshakable great fortune, or whatever kingdom he desires;
he shall happily attain the accomplishments of the earth and the atmosphere.
Then it is known as the Nairājana rite, which brings about supreme and all-encompassing welfare;
O Goddess, one does not perceive any fault therein as previously described—of this there is no doubt.
One should perform worship among the cows so that the herd always prospers.
A knower of mantras should consecrate either vermilion or yellow ochre with the mantra;
it should be applied to the tips of the horns for the protection of the cows, as it conquers all defects.
For the sake of protecting horses, one should perform sacrifice according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having consecrated a water-pot with mantras, one should cause it to be placed upon their heads.
Having consecrated white mustard seeds with mantras, one should place them on the neck and on the head;
thus, one shall protect the elephants, which are thereby freed from all defects.
For in this way, animals are protected from enemies;
thus, a king should always ensure protection is provided for all living beings everywhere.
For them there shall be great peace, and famine shall always perish;
even amidst all great terrors, such as falling meteors, earthquakes, and landslides.
Excessive rain, drought, and the portents of fear; flowers and such appearing out of season; and the sky being marred by ruined or shattered celestial bodies.
If the mandala is afflicted by defects such as fever and spiders, by untimely deaths,
and by various kinds of miseries;
Whatever faults of karma there may be, as well as terrible planetary afflictions,
the concealment that has arisen, and likewise any breach in the mantra—
[all these are removed] by the destruction of the entry of the *vaṭa*-tree and so forth, and by [the removal of] insects, boils, and the like.
In disorders of wind and bile, in all types of phlegm imbalances, in hemorrhoids, eye diseases, and in conditions such as erysipelas and carbuncles;
Diseases born of wind, those born of bile, as well as disorders of the bodily constituents (dhātu),
and whatever other various ailments there may be, numbering in the thousands, all arise from injury.
Diseases residing within, sorrows and the like that cause the destruction of thought, and whoever among all [beings], such as Brahmins and others, have been cursed; [all these are overcome].
Then, for the sake of peace, the sacrifice should be performed according to the prescribed sequence;
an oblation should be offered every day for the increase of the king and his kingdom.
They enjoy the kingdom in happiness; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
By merely worshipping [the deity] once, those who create obstacles are destroyed.
Just as deer flee from a lion in all eighteen directions,
poverty is destroyed from one's lineage through the practice of constant application.
In whatever kingdom and in whatever country a knower of mantras always dwells, there pestilences, diseases, khārkhodas, thieves, and malevolent planets do not exist.
Various Śākinīs, Yakṣas, Piśācas, and likewise Rākṣasas;
child-seizing spirits (Bālagrahas), eruptive boils (Visphoṭakas), and those who are Vyantaras and Antaras;
serpents, other afflictions, famine, and the oppression of enemies.
All powers prevail here where this mantra-vidyā is established;
he is always to be honored by all living beings and by kings alike.
If one is honored with incomparable acts such as gifts, worship,
and marks of respect, then by that mere act of honoring, all mantras are indeed honored.
When they are placed at his mouth and duly honored, they bestow happiness there;
yet the planets, as destroyers everywhere, afflict the practitioner.
Therefore, water and rice should be offered to all the planets;
having sacrificed to the spirits, they are satisfied, yet they do not remain satisfied.
Then protection must be performed by the high-souled preceptor.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Protection of Kings," in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, within the section on the rites of Mṛtyujit and Amṛtīśa.
The auspicious Goddess said:
O Lord, protection has been taught out of compassion for living beings;
how is it described, to whom is it performed, and in what manner?
The Puruṣa is declared to be all-pervading, indeed formless, and the embodied one of all living beings;
he dwells both outside and inside the body, devoid of qualities, and is the creator of the bodiless. How then is his protection performed, and from what does he protect?
How, moreover, is this entire body to be protected?
It is said to be composed of and impelled by the great elements, such as earth and the rest.
"O Lord, who is this third one, or what is his demonic nature, and how is he a deity?
Why is he to be protected, and by whom? Tell me, O wielder of the trident."
"O Blessed One, tell me all of this in its entirety: what is the protection?
The Blessed One replied:
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret, which has not been asked of me by gods or asuras,
nor by Garuḍa and others, nor by my many disciples or sages.
I shall now declare that at its beginning and end; listen, O large-eyed one!
The Puruṣa is all-pervading, subtle, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), free from action (niṣkriya), and powerful.
But what is this? It is the threefold impurity consisting of the atomic (āṇava), the karmic (karma), and the illusory (māyīya).
Due to connection with that, [the soul] is indeed defiled, lacking independence, and devoid of power.
Therefore, it is declared to be impure because of its opposition to the three impurities;
or how can it be called stainless when it is opposed to worldly enjoyments?
One who possesses enjoyments while remaining pure does not attain perfection; "enjoyment" is said to be conceptual construction.
That conceptual construction is indeed saṃsāra, the constant wandering of the bound soul (paśu).
However, for one who is transmigrating and bound, the state of being stainless is logical;
for that subtle *āṇava* impurity is indeed perceived through its effects.
Desire, however, is its effect; it is that which sets in motion enjoyments and the like.
Action is the instrument whose effects arise from place, time, and the body.
The wise know that everything from the earth downwards is the effect of Māyā;
thus, endowed with the three impurities, the individual soul (aṇu) wanders in saṃsāra.
Just as a silkworm firmly entombs itself within its cocoon,
so too is the self capable of being released from the cage of bonds through the process of disentangling.
As long as the powerful Lord God does not bestow His grace,
so long does the bound soul (paśu) remain enveloped and obscured by the shroud of impurity (mala).
If there were no Lord at all, and the entire world were independent,
then there would be no regulation of causes, which would be irrational.
Just as when someone binds a bull with a rope, that animal is rendered dependent through the enjoyment of grass and fodder; so too is the person.
Just as no one is seen who is capable of seizing this [noose] while it is held in his hand, so too the Lord is the bestower of grace.
And Śiva, empowered by his own power, is capable of [bestowing] all [these fruits] simultaneously;
that [power] is inseparable from him, like the innate rays of the sun.
Just as heat, which causes burning and illumination, is never separated from fire,
so too that auspicious power (śakti) of the Lord is inseparable and identical with Śiva.
O Goddess, she is the cause of the universe; though she is one, she exists in many ways.
She abides in the forms of will, knowledge, and action, according to the differentiation of her functions.
That non-terrible (aghorā) will be His will, all-pervasive and joy-bestowing;
but that which consists of terrible ignorance is the one abiding in grasping.
Another is devoted to the terrible and the non-terrible; she is the nature of action belonging to Kṣobhikā.
She is the protection of all beings, the protector of all protections.
And that initiation is declared to be characterized by the gift of a *paṇa*;
in this very manner, it is the destroyer of all defects.
For the all-pervading person (puruṣa) who already exists, that protection is not prescribed;
however, I shall further proclaim another protection, the "Protector of All Protections."
Due to the non-contradiction of the three [times], the various fruits of karma arise;
thus, the sense faculties proceed toward their objects, such as sound and the rest.
Situated in the center of the heart-lotus, it is the impeller of both dharma and adharma;
it is overcome by passion and hatred, and is enveloped by the threefold internal organ.

The relationship between cause and effect, bound together by the senses and the elements, is not at all attached to the impurity of consciousness, even hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of times.
By those [factors] consisting of what is to be done and what is not to be done, and by the deliberations on dharma and adharma, consciousness is obscured;
that is designated as the *jīva*.
She has been designated as "Red" by Śiva, the Supreme Self, through various extensive mantras, as well as through the mantras and tantras of dhāraṇā.
O Maheśvara, that which is called the protection of the vital breath (jīva) is the power of action (kriyā-śakti);
the other, the third protection, is the protection of the body.
From all great fears, from *bhūtas*, *yakṣas*, *grahas*, and the like,
as well as from *ḍākas*, *ḍāmarikas*, the sisters (*bhaginyas*), and likewise Māra.
Śākinīs and Yoginīs certainly inflict various kinds of violence by means of mouth-bites, *maṇḍakas*, and other such methods.
That which pacifies whatever fear there may be is called protection and power;
[it concerns] the body born of the elements, which is impure, unstable, and impermanent.
The body is corrupted by hundreds of various defects, such as wind, bile, phlegm, and combinations thereof.
For many malevolent beings with wicked intentions afflict him—
those born of wind, bile, disease, spirits, phlegm, and the combination of all three humors.
Others likewise desire food, desire praise, and desire pleasure;
some desire to kill, while others carry weapons and are harmful toward all living beings.
