For those born of wind (vāta) indeed prevail by taking recourse to the seat of wind;
those born of bile (pitta) then agitate their own seat and likewise that of the bile.

Those born of phlegm disturb their own state, and those born of the combination of all three humors disturb their station, for the sake of destruction; therefore, the protection of the body [is necessary].
Protection, impelled by Śiva, must indeed be practiced through the application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and ritual actions;
it is eternally bestowing grace upon Śiva and is the remover of both auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.

O dear one, those who desire to return are devoured by voracious beings accompanied by their followers; those who wish to enjoy [them] seek to kill them, yet they perish through the power of mantra and yoga.
Likewise, those who desire pleasure [are overcome] by many mantras, tantras, and medicinal herbs.
Even though he was addressed with favor by that mantra-practitioner,
those desires which were proclaimed— difficult to overcome and possessed of great strength— took hold of him.
Nevertheless, by the power of the splendor of the supreme mantra of the Lord, and through the majesty of Śiva’s Śakti, they are destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, this determination of the elements has been briefly proclaimed;
it is shown here in detail for the benefit of living beings.
For in this way, when well-understood, protection is truly accomplished;
otherwise, it leads even the practitioner to his own destruction.
Various types of protection must be performed according to the traditional teachings:
first, the protection of the support; second, the protection of the life-force.
The third is the protection of the womb; at the time of childbirth, one should perform the fourth;
the fifth is the protection against *bhūtas*; having bathed, one should then perform the sixth.
The seventh is declared for children, and likewise the eighth for men.
I shall explain their distinction so that one may appoint them according to their capacity;
those who contemplate reality must ensure the protection of mothers and fathers.
Having committed offenses against a virtuous person, those who would harm him arise;
for he is one who must be protected with effort for the sake of his well-being, yet they seek to injure him.
When a woman is sealed by the bhūtas, then the embryo is not conceived;
this is proclaimed as the first protection, known as the "Foundation."
Since the body of all living beings consists of blood,
the practitioners of mantra must, at that time, protect these two.
And for those seized by the desire for pleasure, who engage in amorous conduct in manifold ways,
how can it be that they drink [the] emitted semen at night and yet conceive?
Therefore, for that reason, the semen must be protected so that conception may occur; once conceived, the embryo must be guarded against miscarriage.
At the time of childbirth, protection for women should be diligently provided by those skilled in protective rites; thus, malevolent beings will not cause them harm.

As long as the woman who has recently given birth has not become pure, the infant staying in that house is afflicted by the defects of the *sūtikā* and the *grahas*; [therefore, one should protect him] with [the following] ritual.

Therefore, a wise person should ensure that both the woman who has recently given birth and the child staying with her are well-protected by means of mantras, weapons, and other such measures at the time of the ritual bath.
Powerful beings cause harm; therefore, one should perform the ritual bath.
Having bathed, at that subsequent time, [one should practice] the protection of children.
The nurse, however, is the cause for that [growth] through nourishment such as the contact with milk;
therefore, the child must be protected from the nurse and others thereafter.
One should protect [the patient] at all times through the application of mantras and medicinal herbs,
as well as by means of dhāraṇīs, meditations, mudrās, consecrations, and incenses.
Having performed oblations with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other substances, and having consecrated [the person] on the head with various auspicious jars, he must be protected at all times.
He saw him as a child, as one awakened from sleep, weeping, laughing, eating,
lying on his bed, standing, and likewise playing.
At dawn, at midnight, at midday,
and at all times of twilight, she should protect that young child.
At the time of twilight, there is a gathering of gods, asuras, spirits, mothers, sisters, and beloved grahas and piśācas.
During all the twilights, the child must be protected;
whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, one should guard him at all times.
O Goddess, those who desire to kill will seek to slay you as you go along;
but while you remain here, protected, they shall not harm you, for they are most terrifying.
While he is healthy and sleeping at the proper time, these lowest of planetary spirits terrify him from all sides;
yet when he is awake at night, they alone cause him terror.
Therefore, O Dear One, one should always protect the child with every effort,
and by no other means or incantations except for this.
Indeed, the prince must be protected with special care by his teachers;
for he is endowed with auspicious fortune, possesses excellent qualities, and is guarded by all the marks of excellence.
Having seen [it], they strive with effort to kill the auspicious infant;
therefore, immediately thereafter, one should protect it in every possible way through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās).
Or, O Goddess, by means of a wall-weapon, or by various auspicious mantras,
or by means of written yantras and yogas, one should perform the worship with great effort.
With threads of white and other colors wound around or fastened to the neck,
with various kinds of incense, and likewise with those wearing jewels;

Young girls, and especially princes, must always be protected with protective *tilaka* marks, as well as by *nīrājanā* and *sarā* rites; likewise, O beloved, the five queens and the king’s mother should perform recitations of mantras for their protection.
By this very method, she must be protected with firm resolve by those for whom the minor spirits,
the great elements, and the mothers who harbor evil thoughts [pose a threat].
They constantly and tirelessly strive with great effort to kill;
out of compassion for living beings, [I act] for the sake of pacifying them.
Mantras, medicinal herbs, and those [beings] of great strength and prowess—
have all been brought down by me for the sake of bestowing grace upon mortals.
Indeed, from the vast splendor of all those mantras,
there arise strength, vigor, as well as knowledge, memory, intelligence, and eloquence.
I have declared that the Lord is the life of all and the conqueror of death,
[attained] through abundant sacrifices, recitations, fire-offerings, austerity, and self-restraint.
Mantras and weapons achieve success in accordance with the nature of the age;
likewise, in this degenerate age, people are wicked and most sinful, by which they are overcome.
For them, those mantras may or may not grant success;
however, for this God of gods, they remain effective throughout the duration of the Kṛta and other ages.
For those whose nature conforms to [true] being, austerity does not arise from the practice of vows;
for those who are serene in all states of being, who seek to conquer both duality and non-duality,
yet are possessed of misfortune and laziness, their minds are struck down by evil.
O Bandha, there is no doubt that you possess the power of mere devotion;
just as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) grants every desired object when thought of.
In the same way, indeed, every eye performs its function for one who has cultivated [the mind],
just as the sun and moon appear equally in the world to all.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these indeed function collectively through the heart with the thought, "We shall consume food."
Likewise, the Supreme Lord is all-pervading within all beings;
free from phenomenal manifestation, he is the Sovereign who bestows everything upon all.
O Supreme God, conqueror of death, the bestower of all accomplishments upon all;
one who relies solely on devotion and is intent upon meditation and concentration [attains this].
He who knows this and has attained it with an unwavering mind obtains the entire fruit and becomes one who ascends to all perfections.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Section on Desired Planetary Transits and so forth," within the *Mṛtyujid-amṛtīśa-vidhāna* of the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*.
The Goddess said:
"Everything that I had not asked has been told to me by Your Majesty;
now I wish to hear about the doubt residing in my heart."
How do those *yoginīs*, as well as the *rākṣasīs* and *śākinīs* who are proud of their power,
draw forth the life-breaths from another's body in an instant?
And why are they pitiless and fierce, or what is their purpose?
O Blessed One, you ought to explain all of this in detail.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret:
how they intend to take the lives [of those who oppose] by the command of the Lord of Beasts.
Free from passion and hatred, and devoid of greed and delusion,
they sprinkle those animals for the sake of the sacrifice of the God of Gods.
They do not harm out of greed, nor indeed with the intent to kill;
they abide in the command of the god Mahābhairava.
For this purpose, the Self-born One himself touched the sacrificial animals;
otherwise, animals would not offer themselves for the sacrifice to the Lord.
O fair-faced one, for the sake of favoring those beings and animals,
they indeed liberate them from their sins and sever the multitude of their bonds.
For those animals that have been utilized, one should always maintain a mind directed toward the Supreme;
by the command of Śiva, they are joined through the threefold yoga.
For others do not indeed join them with even a subtle [weapon] through their own threefold [means],
nor do they strike them down by force in this case.
That which is supreme, existing within the all-encompassing reality, free from limitation and pure,
is the pervasive nature of the Supreme Lord— the cause of all causes.
Situated within that interval, it bestows grace upon all;
in that very place, those stainless ones, free from weariness, are appointed.
They have attained a state of oneness and are not separated in any way;
yet, when that power dissolves, they remain established in the form of the [original] shadow.
Those whose excellence is known, who abide in the stage of ritual action, and who are *avadhūtīs* fit for sacrifice—
having firmly established themselves in that state, they unite [the practitioner] with that very form.
Those who are liberated and have become Śiva, being devoted to Śiva through their practice,
become stainless and, by His power, they truly become Śiva.
Just as the state of Śiva is attained through initiation by means of yoga,
so indeed does one reach the state of Śiva through the practice of yoga.
For this aforementioned candidate, who is utterly defiled and whose nature is obscured by impurity, these [powers] bring about stainlessness.
For by cutting off the root, one seeks to destroy the three impurities; once the body of the impurity has been destroyed, it does not sprout again.

For that bound soul (paśu), initiation alone is the means of union; there is no such thing as "slaying" [the soul], for it occurs through the pervasive nature of the Self and the expansion of one's own power.
They tear apart the snares of the snarer; the body perishes.
When the body has perished, there is liberation, not the desire for killing.
For a person who is bound by firmly entangled snares,
the wise know that separation from the body results in death.
Now, another method is being described, which is indeed subtle;
this knowledge, consisting of subtle power, is praised by means of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

Those perfected ones worship that knowledge which bestows supernatural powers, which reaches the end through the resonance of the sound "arā-arā-varā-viṣṭya," and which is illuminated by the light of sound. They worship it by means of the Khecarī mudrā.
The knowledge of bound souls (paśus) is shrouded by ignorance and remains situated in impurity;
however, those goddesses indeed prevail through stainless knowledge.
Just as one who has fallen asleep plays here and there upon waking,
or just as one intoxicated by the consumption of liquor wanders about somewhere, so too does the fool play or wander here and there due to his lack of self-mastery.
Or one who is insane may be impelled by a heedless person,
or by mothers, guhyakas, or by one's own power through the strength of yoga.
By the power of yoga, the life-force of animals is swiftly drawn forth—
that which is supreme, unmanifest, eternal, immovable, and constant.
Having entered that [body] from another's body by means of the path of yoga, and having become transcendent, one should envelop the life-force with one's own life-force through one's own power.
Having ascended that [channel] from the seat of the heart and entered through the upper path,
one should attain oneness and practice equanimity therein.
Relying upon the supreme cause, one should thoroughly practice autonomy;
through the pervasive essential nature, one should bring both power and powerlessness under control.
Then, O Goddess, one who knows the yoga of installation should perform the *śānticcheda* within that casket (*saṃpuṭa*), and thereafter establish the *tattva* in the form of Śakti.
One should heat [the object] by means of the sun of consciousness in the form of the existence of one's own essential nature;
then, standing beyond that, one should liquefy it within the rays like the sun.
One should unite within the heart all the sense organs, beginning with sound,
as well as the elements that have become the objects of taste, and indeed all the qualities in every respect.
Therefore, having grasped the aggregate of the instruments with the mind,
the yogi should then enter, assailing that city from every side.
Having quickly grasped all of that, one should swiftly bring it into one's own self;
at that very moment, one should bring forth the life-force through the application of mudrās and mantras.
By this method, the yogi should practice subtle yoga;
through subtle yoga, the knower of yoga shall swiftly attain all of that.
The subtle yoga has been fully explained, and now the gross [yoga] is being described:
by means of the practice of the *piṇḍastha* [state], one shall certainly draw forth the *piṇḍa*.
By means of the ritual application of mantras and mudrās, according to the prescribed rule,
and through the power of meditative yoga, as well as by the characteristics of the *cchummaka* and other [secret] signs.
Those whose doubt has been resolved [dwell] in the city of the fettered beings (*paśu*);
however, the yogins, proud of their power, [attain it] through the threefold yoga.
O Goddess, when they seek to strike you down, then one should practice what is beneficial;
[one should worship] Death, the god who is falsehood and whose face is turned everywhere.
Having understood that supreme yoga through its very own nature as all-pervasive, the knower of mantras, the practitioner, pervades the city of the bound soul.
Having understood the sequence of the yogis, the mantra-master, skilled in exertion, should protect his auspicious life, which is sustained by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
O illustrious one, for all those aforementioned harmful beings,
[one should] through yoga, by means of one's own power, [apply] the subtle wheel.
By means of the previously mentioned severing of the knot through subtle meditation, the knower of mantras shall liberate [the practitioner] from all defects; it can never be otherwise.
Endowed with the power of the sacrifice of knowledge, he is proficient in mantras and tantras;
he has conquered death, is accomplished in mantra, is an ascetic, and has his senses fully restrained.
Endowed with meditation, mantras, and so forth, established in goodness, wise, and powerful, he is the supreme yogi, contented and devoted to the eightfold form.
Freed from passion and hatred, devoid of greed and delusion,
he is indeed fearless, free from doubt, and devoted solely to bestowing grace.
O beloved, he who releases one from the aforementioned terrible defects becomes a liberator;
otherwise, he is merely a destroyer of the essence of being.
The wicked one who brings ruin to his own family is certainly cooked in hell;
likewise, various malevolent spirits and harmful beings [afflict] the tree.
Yoginīs, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, and those who cause misfortune—
some desire to devour me, while others likewise desire me.
The Ratis, Kāmas, Sādhyas, Skanda and others, the Brahmarākṣasas,
and whatever countless others there may be from the Raurava hell— [he does not stay] anywhere with them.

The hero [of the story] should be composed by those who know themselves, who are wise regarding their own welfare, who seek wealth, and who are diligent; but it should not be made by those who seek fame.
Out of compassion, one should certainly cause the construction of temples for Śiva, Candra, and the others,
in every way for kings, their sons, and [their] grandsons.
In whatever country or kingdom a knower of yoga and mantra resides,
there the king is the lord and that deity is the preceptor of the hermitages.
The king becomes the preceptor for all the stages of life;
though he abides in the Kṛta age, he endures those who are his mothers.
Those previously mentioned fierce and terrible [omens] will entirely subside through the offering of garlands and through abundant sacrifices performed by those kings.
They satisfy [all beings] and would tolerate everything;
indeed, those who contemplate Śiva should not engage in the practice of mantra at all times.
Listen now to the praise of those terrible beings who, by various means, destroy the body composed of the five elements.
By means of the gross through the gross state— using powders, incenses, and ointments,
as well as the application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and ritual procedures preceded by the induction of possession.
And by the application of mechanical devices (*yaṃtra*) and wheels (*cakra*), as well as by the protection of living beings (*jīvarakṣā*) and the like,
by battle-strategies, and by the retention of perfected mantras (*siddhamantra*).

By those who know the rituals of mudrās and mantras, by those who contemplate the coming and going [of breath], by heroes skilled in the rituals of the *bhūta*-tantras, and by those well-reflecting experts in medicinal herbs;
By those who are self-controlled, vigilant, free from confusion,
devoted to morning ablutions, performing worship, and intent upon recitation and meditation.

The recitation of mantras must be performed by those who know the one hundred thousand characteristics, who are free from expectations, who are highly skilled, and who are contemplative; it should not be done otherwise.
If one desires supreme accomplishment or eternal, certain liberation, one must not engage in the practice of mantras; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
For the sake of favoring mortals, kings,
and the wicked, one who desires their welfare should perform [this] while established in his position.
If one should ever perform [the rite] without continuity, he perishes;
those who are empowered and devoted to the sacrifices of Śiva do not tolerate it.
Constantly free from fear and obedient to the command of Bhairava,
those who have received his command carry it out through the application of mantras and mudrās.
They do not seek to kill for their own sake; therefore they are remembered as powerful. Long ago, O God, they were [conquered] by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
For by this method, sixteen classes of Piśācas were created;
possessed by that power, they were generated as exceedingly strong.
O Goddess, having seen the fourteenfold creation, those [beings] were formerly set in motion by the Self-born One with the intent to destroy it and to consume it.
Since they were created by him in the past, mantras of unfailing power—
seven crores in number and possessed of great strength— stand on his side.
Those who are wicked, terrible to the world, and seeking to kill with their excessive strength— for the sake of subduing them and for the sake of protecting the world— [I shall act].
The application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and ritual actions— whether numbering one hundred or more—
has been commanded by the Supreme Lord; their practice is indeed for that purpose alone,
in all mantra-discourses, and not otherwise when the command is transgressed.
And by its power, mantras are strong and possess unfailing efficacy;
yet, apart from that potency, the remaining phonemes are merely [sounds].
It is proclaimed as the conqueror of death; it is the Lord, the sovereign of all mantras.
No other mantra or vidyā can override its command.
Through recollection, they become as fickle as deer [in the presence of] a hunter's trap.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Authority on the Attraction of the Life-force and so forth," within the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, in the section concerning the rites of Death and the Lord of Immortality.
And may there be prosperity!
O Lord, what is the nature of mantras? What is their true form and of what kind are they?
What is their power, how are they effective, and by whom indeed are they employed?
And those whose nature is Śiva are all-pervasive and have the form of emptiness;
since they are devoid of a cause, how indeed can there be agency for them?
Since they are formless, how can their agency be possible?
O Lord, tell me: who can perform an action without a body?
For the Supreme Lord is never seen as bodiless;
since he is bound by a body, how can there be agency for one who is bound? Due to impurity, he is perceived as lacking independence and having his powers eclipsed.
The agency of one who lacks power is contradictory in all things;
likewise, how can mantras whose essence is Śiva be effective in reality?
If there exists that which has the nature of power, to whom does that power belong and of what kind is it?
O Lord, is power the cause, or is the effect of whom and of what kind?
Who is this "possessor of power" (*śaktimān*) to whom some power is attributed? Independence cannot be established without some [entity] that is already established.
But that which is established by means of what is unestablished is itself declared to be unestablished;
for in this regard, power is indeed established only in some cases where there is an absence of a real entity.
Those mantras, however, are merely of the nature of power (śakti),
whereas the Vedāṇava mantras possess the form of embodied bodies.
The powerful do not indeed wash away the powerful, for they are of the same essential nature; who can wash away whom? Only the impure can wash away the impure.
The mantras are not established as independent from the Siddhas; they are the Supreme Lord himself.
In that state, the threefold nature is destroyed, and there is a stable abiding in non-duality.
In this matter, one should employ reason alone out of a desire for the welfare of living beings;
for mantras are seen to be powerful and indeed unassailable by gods or asuras.
Since you are indeed all-pervading at all times by virtue of being the benefactor of all,
O Great Lord, please speak to me briefly regarding my doubt.
O Lord of the World, there is nothing whatsoever other than you;
O Lord of the Gods, tell me everything, if you are pleased with me, O Master.
The Blessed One said:
This great secret of the *Tha* [mantra] has not been asked about by anyone;
yet I have always exhorted everyone regarding it in all the scriptures.
Those of deluded soul, perpetually veiled by illusion, do not perceive it;
without the three principles, it is not possible to speak of it.
Let alone the entire world; until that reality is realized, everything whatsoever that is perceived here is constructed from the three principles.
O Goddess, indeed no category of existence exists without these three principles;
therefore, all things—both the supreme and the non-supreme—are comprised within these three principles.
Having Śiva as their essence, being of the nature of Śakti, and likewise having the mantras as their essence,
they indeed exist with immeasurable splendor through the division of the three principles (tattvas).
But the supreme, all-pervading, primordial, eternal cause is free from phenomenal expansion,
indefinable, incomparable, and free from affliction.
It is without appearance, supremely peaceful, free from all afflictions, all-pervading,
auspicious in every respect, and endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
Filled with a mass of gnosis, delighted by the bliss of its own bliss,
it is beyond bliss, free from conceptual construction, devoid of ritual conduct, and beyond syllables.
Non-duality, devoid of conceptual construction, the radiance of consciousness that removes the impurities of consciousness,
pervading both the conscious and the unconscious— this has arisen as the unsurpassed reality.
Unchanging, supreme, eternal, stainless, and free from affliction;
devoid of all measurement and abandoned by all states of being.
All forms transcend the parts; it is immovable and eternal.
O Mantra of the Parts, you are devoid of worlds and syllables.
Abiding within all beings and established in all beings, all mantras reside therein; the all-pervading Lord is contained within everything.
The giver of all, abiding in all states of being, the forest of all [existence],
situated in the hearts of all beings, the impeller among all creatures.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, nothing whatsoever is seen that is devoid of Him;
therefore, He alone is the Supreme Lord, the all-pervading universe.
The omniscient one—his awakening is indeed beginningless;
he is the independent Maheśvara, whose powers are both withdrawn and infinite.
And the will of that Maheśvara is in every way free from conceptual construction.
Since it is immeasurable and beginningless, how can it be attained?
For, in reality, it is comprehended through inference based on its effects.
His supreme power is his effect, just as rays belong to the sun;
it should be understood as being like the heat of fire, for they exist in a state of inseparable concomitance.
She is the Dakari, auspicious, following the will of Śiva;
she possesses his nature, is tranquil, eternal, and characterized by grace.
All this is indeed an illusory manifestation (vivarta), which must arise from that [Supreme Reality] through its power and not from anything else;
she is with bliss (sānanda), while the supreme Śiva is beyond bliss (nirānanda).
The qualities of Śiva, the Supreme Self, such as omniscience and the rest, are seen by him through Śakti; for they cannot be established otherwise.
Śiva is one, and likewise Śakti is one;
she is eternal, established in duality, and she alone is the source of all things.
This [power] of Śiva is indeed his will-form (icchārūpā), non-different from him and facing in all directions;
it is the attainment of a slight state of swelling, which constitutes the qualities such as omniscience and the rest.
But when that very same [consciousness] alone awakens everything within form,
that awakening which is indeed beginningless is remembered as the supreme knowledge.
Known as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), she is the locus of qualities such as omniscience; though independent, that power takes the form of the cause of action (*kriyā*).
That Mātṛkā, whose form consists of sound beginning with 'Sya' and so forth, through the eightfold division of the forms of the vowels (vaṣṭarūpa),
is designated as the power of grace belonging to Maheśvara.
That supreme [reality] is indeed called action, yet it is formless;
thus it is said to be "done," though it is one, not other, and born of its own nature.
Arising from her own nature, she is indeed of the nature of self; auspicious, she is proclaimed as arisen from herself. She is not at all distinct [from him], nor is she called the agent.
Since Śiva is perfectly complete, autonomous, and all-pervasive, who could be his agent or disturber? That very state of being Śiva belongs to him alone.
That which constitutes his state of being the creator of all is metaphorically designated as "power" (śakti),
by means of which he effects creation, maintenance, dissolution, and withdrawal.
The Blessed One performs every act of concealment and grace;
by his power of action he creates, and by his power of knowledge he maintains the stability of the world.
Rudra effects withdrawal through his nature of *māyā*,
while grace is performed by Jyeṣṭhā; thus is the collection of names [established],
since the fivefold activity of Śambhu exists for the sake of the world’s manifestation.
Nothing at all is to be conceptualized through action; rather, it is known [directly]. Therefore, this power is inferred as belonging to Śiva alone.
The Self is indeed the infinite God, yet it is obstructed by impurity;
however, those [souls] are seized by the supreme will of the Supreme Lord.
Likewise, the Self and the three principles are to be known as the supreme;
and likewise, the God Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha are of a threefold nature.
He effects a sixfold creation, divided into four categories:
[the realms of] hell-beings, animals, spirits, gods, and humans.
O Goddess, the all-pervading Lord performs everything according to his power— whether it be the womb-born, the egg-born, the sweat-born, or the soil-born— by means of his sovereign power.
The deity is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), just as [the potter is to the jar];
however, that power is the material cause (*upādāna*) by virtue of its inherence (*samavāya*) in the eye.
Just as the great sun-crystal gem, through contact with the rays of the sun,
produces fire for a purpose, yet there is no causal agency (*kāraṇatva*) belonging to either of the two.
When the magnet-stone sees iron, it acts with affection toward it;
yet there is no desire in either of them, for such is merely the causal condition.
Because of its subtlety, that which impels those two would not be perceived;
such a self is neither an end nor a cause of destruction for beings.
That power, however, is perceived as the appropriation (upādāna) everywhere;
just as everything is seen to be perfectly accomplished through the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
The wise know that the state of the agitated and the agitator, as well as the conjunction at the side-limit, is the cause.
One should create everything, including all that is moving and unmoving, by one's power and without desire;
in this manner, according to the prescribed rule, all mantras are born from the three principles (tattvas).
And likewise, they are of the nature of power (*śakti*) and identical with the essential nature of the Self;
they are declared to possess the three natures and are powerful everywhere.
They all exist as givers of everything, omnipresent, and possessing all forms;
for Śiva is indeed beginningless, the primordial power.
But when, O Lord, they flow forth without delay by His will,
that power is supremely subtle, beyond the mind (unmanā), and possesses the nature of Śiva.
When she consumes the self as mere existence,
she is designated as Samanā, the power that abides throughout all the paths.
She who embraces the universe, having withdrawn it, creates it again—
she is the great power named Kauṇḍilī, indeed the third.
Form, which is the unmanifest body of Śiva, free from duality and expansion,
spreads with extreme velocity and fills the world with sound.
The Lord of the gods of gods is proclaimed as Sadāśiva;
the sound [of the Veda] comes to rest in accordance with him.
O all you gods, among those who have ceased [to act], none is renowned as a restrainer;
yet, in one who has been restrained, the conceit of being a Great Lord arises.
Indeed, countless millions remain [there],
and those who have entered here obtain that which is known as the Lord Bindu.
When the auspicious nectar, the cause of creation, falls upon the crown of the head, one becomes nourished by it; therefore, he is known as "the half-moon."
And indeed, the letter *ma* is the very cause of the creation of all castes;
for here, Rudra is the supreme union of the letters.
When he attains that which is established and oriented toward the cause of emanation,
he truly becomes manifest as the one called Pratiṣṭhā.
But when everything has ceased, they know the perfected Praṇava;
that which is called the syllable *Oṃ* is the supreme, auspicious Brahman, seated upon the lotus.
This emanation of mantras belongs to Śiva, the supreme;
it consists of fifty letters through its eightfold division.
The wise know the supreme, most subtle power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) to be the end of Mātṛkā;
she is the source of all mantras and resides as the friction-stick for all measures.
He offered *laṃ*, which is joined with the creation of nectar;
therefore, he is the Lord of the Gods, the Lord of Nectar (*Amṛteśa*), both transcendent and immanent.
Because he delivers one from death, he is called Mṛtyujit;
because he sustains [all things], he is known as Bhairava.
All these and other mantras are remembered as having the splendor of nectar;
O beloved, they exercise authority over the entire world.
For they liberate those who have fallen into the cycle of existence;
because they possess the nature of protecting from mental affliction, they are therefore known as *mantras*.
Therefore, mantras are omnipresent, existing at all times as the reality of the three truths;
they consist of the nature of Śiva, Śakti, and the Self, and are eternally gracious.
Their powers are bestowers of auspiciousness and removers of inauspiciousness;
for as soon as they are known, they grant fruit, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This is because they possess the nature of all the goddesses and indeed the power of all energies.
That Śiva is the state of power (*śaktitva*), the agency of all,
the agent of grace toward all, and the bestower of fruits everywhere.
Regarding the nature of the self, its threefold means of accomplishment is traditionally taught as mantra, meditation, and likewise mudrā; that [is] the [means].
Initiation, the consecration of the maṇḍala, sacrifice, as well as austerity,
the performance of fire-offerings, the drawing [of the diagram], meditation, and the practice of the concentrations (dhāraṇās).
Likewise, the binding of mudrās, yoga, and sacrifice have been performed;
these mantras are declared to be authoritative in all circumstances.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Investigation of Mantras," within the *Sarvatrasrotasaṃgrahasāra*, concerning the ritual procedure for Mṛtyujit Amṛtīśa.
The illustrious Goddess said:
Indeed, incalculable tens of millions of mantras of immeasurable power have been spoken by the God— mantras that are all-knowing, all-bestowing, all-pervading, and auspicious.
The lords of all are capable and possess authority everywhere;
yet among all of them, he alone is somehow superior and more powerful.
O Lord, how is the Supreme Īśāna, the foremost of the lords of mantras, the Conqueror of Death?
O God, tell me this that has arisen in my heart.
I wish to hear that supreme essence of mantra previously mentioned, which is named after the deity in the heart; I am filled with great curiosity.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, [O Lord], to the doubt residing in my heart:
for by means of ten million mantras, all are indeed authorized in every respect.
And by the power of Śiva’s Śakti, they are endowed with all powers;
strengthened by the strength of the Śaktis of enjoyment and liberation.
But, O Goddess, Śiva is supreme, peaceful, immeasurable, endowed with all virtues, the soul of all, pure, perceivable through devotion, and unsurpassed.
The Supreme Lord is their ultimate support;
produced by His will, they are impelled by His power.
All become givers of fruit, and all are indeed qualified for this very place,
since this is the supreme abode, the dwelling place of all.
The mantras, which have arisen from his power, possess unfailing efficacy;
for he is their eternal controller, leader, and one who has no need of a following.
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, the protector, the cause, the auspicious one;
[he is] the deliverer through one's own mind.
It leads one toward the state of liberation and delivers one from great fear;
because it leads and likewise causes one to perceive, it is called the "eye" (netra).
Life is the very eye within all beings;
the Supreme Lord is like a master unto the entire collection of mantras.
The Praṇava is established as the breath and the life-force of all living beings;
it grasps everything, and one should contemplate Śiva through its constituent parts.
Established in the state of the sixfold *māra*,
he offers everything by means of the *vidyā*, awakened by the syllable *juṃ*.
The essential nature which is self-evident, characterized by perfect satisfaction,
the support of all immortal states, and accompanied by the emission (visarga), is the supreme Śiva.
By that very root-offering of the *pūrṇāhuti*,
she who abides in her own conduct, established in her own nature, and ever-arisen as her own essential form [is realized].
That which is the single, supreme power, consisting of will, knowledge, and action—it is by means of her that he acts; therefore, he is remembered as Śiva.
Joined with the syllables of the Udgītha, it consists of the principles (tattva), phonemes (varṇa), and words (pada);
it comprises the worlds, the kalās, the mantras, and the six very causes themselves.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and [the sixth]—
by means of their own powers, through the renunciation of these six, there is absorption into the seventh.
The letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the Bindu;
the Half-moon, the Nirodhī, the Nāda, and the end of the Nāda.
The Kuṇḍalinī is all-pervasive; she is that which has been [described] by me, as well as the partless reality of the Self, the Power, and likewise the Unmanā.
That which is radiant yet without appearance, the unsurpassed supreme reality, is declared to be the seventh through the abandonment of the six; it is the dissolution-mālā.
All [the deities] are indeed dissolved therein, equal to it by its grace;
for, augmented by its power, they become capable and truly complete.
O beautiful one, I shall explain their sequence, how they dissolve,
from the letter *a* up to the end of the path.
One should consider that all beings are endowed with eight portions (kalās):
accomplishment (siddhi), supernatural power (ṛddhi), splendor (dyuti), fortune (lakṣmī), intelligence (medhā), beauty (kānti), fortitude (dhṛti), and happiness (sukha).
Immediately upon the arising of the Brahma-kalā, [the following] are established:
Rajas, Rakṣā, Rati, Pālī, Aṅka, Atṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā, Vṛddhi, Māyā, Rātrī, Bhrāmaṇī, and likewise Mohanī.
Renowned as Manonmanī, she resides in the left channel (vāmamārga);
these [energies] remain within the portion of Viṣṇu, abiding in the state of dream as far as the end of the throat.
Darkness, delusion, hunger, sleep, disease, fear of death, and old age—these are indeed the non-terrible (*aghorā*) aspects; however, they manifest within the portion of the Terrible (*raudra*).
(***? Up to the state of deep sleep, the Taijasa pervasion is supreme;
likewise, there are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti.
For these parts of the person are established in the Lord,
just as the flames of a fire remain within the fire-drill.
The state of peace is called the Fourth (turyā), which is proclaimed as being named Nāda;
its pervasion extends to Sadāśiva, and within that, it is known as Vyoma, having the nature of emptiness.
O Savior who ferries across the river of worldly existence, you are the Deliverer;
established in the station of the Dvādaśānta, you are known as the Radiance of the Fourth State beyond the transcendent.
These five indeed are the portions of Īśāna, consisting of the causal nature;
this is declared to be the gross Brahmāṇḍa.
I shall indeed describe the path as it truly exists within the mind and speech;
that which was called the "half-moon" is flooded by the *bindu* at its summit.
O Maheśvarī, that which is joined with the *kalā* is declared to be the nectar of power (*śakti-amṛta*);
[it is] Jyotsnā, the most radiant and stainless Śivā.
These indeed are the digits of the half-moon; they are omniscient, established in the Supreme, bound to the enclosure of Vidyā, and adorned by ten million mantras.
The powers of action are pure, auspicious, and stainless:
Bandhunī, Rodhanī, Raudrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā.
For these digits are indeed suppressors; they are suppressors of all gods at all times.
They are eternally satisfied, highly fortunate, and [the ones who are] the [supreme] ones.
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā—
these are the upward-moving [channels] arising from the sound (nāda) of the kalās.
These [energies], endowed with autonomy, reside within the entire [universe];
though they are not distinct from the nature of Śakti, when known, they bestow omniscience.
Subtle and indeed very subtle, born from the nectar of immortality,
all-pervading and renowned— such is the Śakti-tattva.
Bound by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and enveloped by the seat (*āsana*),
these indeed abide in the principle of power (*śaktitattva*), characterized by the limit of pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*).
Pervasive and having the nature of space, she is known as the infinite protectorless one; O Mistress of the Command, she is remembered as the pervasive *kalā*.
Sarvajñā, Sarvadā, Bhadrā, Sādhanā, Aspr̥haṇā, Dhṛti,
and Samanā— these are renowned as the Śiva-kalās.
[They are] Icchā [and so forth], the bestowers of the power of will;
having taken refuge in the Śiva-tattva, they possess the splendor of a perfectly full ocean.
Possessing infinite power, abiding in six locations, subtle, and exceedingly pure;
[these] are the excellent [energies] ending with Samanā, extending to the infinite.
The gross and the subtle, categorized by their distinctions, are traversed by the six causes;
indeed, that which begins with Śakti and ends with Samanā is the domain of subtle consciousness.
But above that, having realized the supreme peace, which is immeasurable and free from affliction, the Guru liberates [the disciple].
Therein, that stainless Self indeed abides supported by its own power;
it is pure consciousness alone, devoid of any substrate, and fully endowed with knowledge and action.
Free from the states of all existing things,
one’s own self is established as having the nature of a stainless crystal;
and the power belonging to that which is situated therein is the bestower of grace.
O Goddess, as long as [the self] does not become Śiva,
so long is it not like a pure lotus [awakened] by the rays of the sun.
As long as everything has not been illuminated, so long does the Lord remain in expansion;
just as by the union with the sun's rays, the lotus blossoms in an instant.
Likewise, through the power of Śiva,
Śiva becomes endowed with qualities such as omniscience, just as Śiva himself is.
It is without appearance, supreme, peaceful, and unsurpassed;
as long as it has not attained fullness, it is said to possess appearance.
That which is indeed the self of activity, when extended,
then grasps the supreme [reality] through the spreading of its rays.
O Goddess of the gods, by discerning [this] in every respect,
one always brings about the true nature of mantras through such knowledge of mantras.
All [these] bestow the fruit of liberation through their respective portions;
yet when the practitioner of mantra does not find that which effects both creation and dissolution, [he fails].
Mantras that exist merely in the form of their rising and setting yield little fruit;
when chanted and meditated upon, they do not bestow enjoyment or liberation.
Impelled by the command of Śiva, they bestow the fruit [of their practice] upon the practitioner when he perceives the processes of origination, maintenance, and withdrawal.
For those mantras of limited power whose nature is subject to rising and setting,
they yield only slight fruit.
Indeed, these [deities] become present before the practitioner;
thus, commanded by the order of Śiva, they have become one with Śiva and bestow Śiva.
Those [qualities] which have departed become faultless through the power of this auspicious Supreme Self.
He who fully understands the distinction between the higher and the lower regarding the god Amṛteśa, the conqueror of death, [attains all].
Before long, there is no doubt that they will attain immortality;
those who have taken refuge in this mantra become ones who have accomplished their purpose.
For by whatever disposition, and with the desire for whatever fruit,
whenever one takes recourse with devotion to whatever [deity], one shall obtain that very fruit.
O Goddess, that which I have declared to you is not otherwise;
for when I was impelled, I am the one who bestows grace upon all.
Through this secret question, all of that has been revealed by me to you;
thus it has been briefly explained. (********?)
It should not be given to those of evil character, nor to the wrathful, nor likewise to the lustful,
nor to those intent on reviling their gurus, nor to those who disparage the gods and mantras.
It is given to atheists and the deceitful who have been excluded from the performance of dharma;
it is not otherwise, even by two sons.

One should not grant the initiation of the *samaya* even to one who is very dear, without first performing the worship of the Guru, the Deity, and the Fire for those devotees who have been duly initiated.
Under no circumstances whatsoever should it be given;
O Goddess of the Gods, by violating this command, the fall of the body will occur.
"If one gives [the initiation] out of delusion, affection, or a desire for wealth, he goes to a terrible hell; such is the command of the Supreme Lord."
By protecting this [teaching], one shall attain perfection;
and by protecting it, O Goddess, one becomes the Supreme Lord, the conqueror of death.
[Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter on the Greatness of the Mantra in the *Mṛtyujid-amṛtīśa-vidhāna*.]
